items.title: Part-file contract: connectors
items.text: This page holds the [function.connector] table of the part-file contract. It is read with part-file.md, which holds the rest of the contract.

items.title: [function.connector]
items.text:
A sub-table of the [[function]] entry it describes (P1): the connector facet's subject is a FunctionTemplate, not the Part, so a part with more than one connector-style function names each one under its own [[function]] entry, never in one top-level table. Maps to the model's connector facet.

[[function]]
name = "x1"
kind = "connector"
symbol = "connector-fixed"
ports = [{ name = "1", role = "generic", symbol_port = "in" }, { name = "2", role = "generic", symbol_port = "out" }]

[function.connector]
style = "header-2p"
pincount = 2
gender = "male"
Field Type Meaning style string pincount integer At least 1 gender string Optional. A Gender value: "male", "female", "neutral". Absent means not stated, which is not neutral (model-0080) marking string Optional. The label printed on the part, e.g. "X1". Omit it to print the function's name; write "" for no label, and the connector's pins print under the item mates list of strings Optional. The MPNs of the parts this connector mates with, e.g. ["DEMO-HSG-4M"]. Data only: no check reads it yet (parts-0016)

Port names are unique within a function. Two functions of one part may share a port name unless they would print one designation (PORT_NAME_SHARED, parts-0005): a labelled connector function (its marking, else its name; marking = "" is no label) prints -<label> behind the item's designation only when the part has two or more labelled connector functions, so X1:1 and X2:1 differ, and so do a clamp group's 1 and X1:1, while a clamp group and a lone labelled connector sharing 1 collide. The lint and the build ask the same segment rule (derive.connector_segments). Two connectors of one part never print one label (CONNECTOR_MARKING_REUSED). A pin prints as -<item>-<label>:<pin>, e.g. -A1-X1:1 (decisions parts-0003, model-0071).

items.title: A header pin that joins a function port
items.text:
A port of a connector function may carry joins = "<function>.<port>". It names a port of another function of the same part (parts-0017).

{ name = "1", role = "generic", symbol_port = "in", joins = "k1.A1" }

The header ports are named by position, "1" to "n", and the printed pin text goes in marking. The join is stored once, on the header port's template. It is a connection with no conductor: net closure puts both ports on one net.

Three lints, all ERROR: - JOIN_PORT_UNKNOWN: the target is no port of the part, or the value is malformed. - JOIN_INTO_CONNECTOR: the target is a port of a connector function. - JOIN_PORT_TWICE: one function port is joined by two header pins.

A header position that repeats another function's port name is PORT_NAME_SHARED.

items.title: A contact part
items.text: A crimp contact is a part file with a [part] table and no [[function]], as a fuse link is (DEMO-CRIMP-F, DEMO-CRIMP-M). A design fits it with contacts= on a connector item (guide/harnesses.md); the BOM counts it once per used pin (model-0170). It has no family or gauge field yet.

items.title: Part-file contract
items.text: Version 1. Parts are data, not code: TOML files in a data package that the loader reads and the lint checks.

items.title: Purpose and audience
items.text: This contract is for someone writing a part library without reading Fransys's source. A part library is a Python data package of TOML files and no code. This document is enough to write one that fransys_parts.load and fransys_parts.lint accept.

items.title: Library layout
items.text:
<library-package>/
  __init__.py
  library.toml
  parts/
    relay-2co-24vdc.toml
    terminal-feedthrough-2_5.toml
    cable-4g1_5.toml
    ...
  • __init__.py carries a one-line docstring and no code: it only makes the directory importable by load(package).
  • library.toml sits at the package root and describes the library as a whole.
  • Every part lives in its own file under parts/. The loader ignores the filename; a lowercased, hyphenated MPN or short description is expected.
  • TOML is read with stdlib tomllib and parse_float=Decimal. No other file format is accepted.

items.title: library.toml fields
items.text: Field Type Meaning schema integer The part-file schema version this library is written against. See "Versioning" below name string The library's name, recorded on the model so a drawing states which library it used version string The library's own version, recorded alongside name description string Free text, not read by the loader

items.title: Part file tables
items.text:
Every part file carries schema = 1 at the top, then the tables below. Fields named here match the model's records (the core kinds and the facets); a field not listed there is out of contract.

Any field below typed as "a <Name> value" takes the string value of a member of that enum in fransys_model.vocab.enums. That module is the authority: the allowed-values lists in this contract are copied from it and can go stale, the module cannot.

items.title: [part]
items.text:
One per file. Maps to the model's Part.

Field Type Meaning mpn string Manufacturer part number. The only home of this fact once loaded manufacturer string description string category string A PartCategory value: "electromechanical", "protection", "terminal", "cable", "connector", "plc_module", "board", "generic" class_code string 1 to 3 uppercase letters, IEC 81346-2:2019, seeding numbering, e.g. "K", "Q", "QA", "X", "W". The first letter is one of B C E F G H J K M N P Q R S T U W X; A, I and O are forbidden and D, L, V, Y and Z reserved (parts lint) operated_by string Optional. An OperatedBy value, what operates the part's contacts as sold: "push", "mushroom", "turn", "position" (parts-0020). A head sold apart from its blocks states it and has no function; its blocks join it with parent=

items.title: [[function]]
items.text:
Zero or more per file, one array entry per function the part has. Maps to the model's FunctionTemplate, with nested ports mapping to PortTemplate and nested links mapping to InternalLink.

Field Type Meaning name string Function name, stamped onto every instance, e.g. "coil", "co_1" kind string A FunctionKind value: "coil", "contact_no", "contact_nc", "contact_co", "protection", "switch", "terminal", "connector", "plc_channel", "supply", "load", "sensor", "actuator", "generic", "bar" symbol string Optional. Symbol key: a lowercase, hyphenated slug naming a symbol in electrical-symbols. A function with no symbol gets no authored layout.symbol_choice, and the layout engine's rules by kind apply energy string Optional, on a supply or load function only: "in" or "out". Default: load in, supply out. Any other kind fails lint (ENERGY_ON_NON_POWER) ports array of tables See below. At least one entry, except a bar cut to length (below) links array of tables See below. Optional; omit for a function with no internal connectivity

A bar writes one port per screw, role "pe"; one cut to length writes none, and each landing makes a screw. It takes no symbol (BAR_SYMBOL): a bar is never drawn.

ports entries:

Field Type Meaning name string The part's own terminal marking, e.g. "13", "A1". Unique within the part, except pins of connectors that print a label. Name a terminal as the device prints it (IN1+, OUT-); where printed names repeat on the part, by its function, numbered (L, N, PE, 24V1, GND1, S24V, F24V1) (owner 2026-09-26, parts-0005) role string A PortRole value: "generic", "internal", "external", "pe", or a throw role "common", "break" (closed at rest), "make" (closed when operated). Every port of a contact_co function takes a throw role, whatever its pin name (CHANGEOVER_ROLE, decisions model-0091, parts-0007) symbol_port string Optional. The role-named port of symbol this port maps to, e.g. "in", "out". A port with no symbol_port keeps its own name. A symbol_port on a function with no symbol is a lint error (SYMBOL_PORT_WITHOUT_SYMBOL). A contact_co port takes none: the drawing binds a changeover by its throw roles (CHANGEOVER_SYMBOL_PORT) marking string Optional. What a drawing prints on this pin, when it differs from name. Omit it to print name; write "" to print nothing side string Optional: "line" or "load"; else the marking fills it (parts-0010). A two-port function that a series passes through needs it when its marking gives no side conductor string Optional: "L1", "L2", "L3", "N", "L+", "L-", "M"; not "PE" (use role = "pe"), filled likewise source_row string Optional. The wiring row a wire on this pin takes, a WiringRow value: "DC_SUPPLY", "DC_GROUND", "DC_CONTROL", "DC_SIGNAL", "AC_L1", "AC_L2", "AC_L3", "AC_N", "AC_CONTROL". Omit it to let the build resolve the row from the pin's net (model-0260); a wire= row map overrides it

links entries:

Field Type Meaning a string A name from this function's ports b string A name from this function's ports kind string A LinkKind value: "conductive", "switched" or "protective" rest string Optional, switched only: "open" or "closed"

A protective link is a fuse or breaker, closed in service. It ends the physical net but not the supply rail (decision model-0122). An overload's main path is conductive.

In a contact_co function, every switched link joins the common port to a break or a make port (CHANGEOVER_LINK).

Rest state (decision parts-0008): a contact_no or contact_nc may omit rest and must agree if it writes it. A switch or generic function must write rest. Lint, all ERROR: SWITCHED_LINK_WITHOUT_REST, REST_DISAGREES_WITH_KIND, REST_ON_UNSWITCHED_LINK, CONTACT_WITHOUT_SWITCHED_LINK, and SYMBOL_REST_MISMATCH (make-contact is open and break-contact and emergency-stop closed).

items.title: [[supply]]
items.text:
Zero or more per file. Maps to the model's supply facet, which allows many per part.

Field Type Meaning supplier string supplier_part_number string note string Optional

items.title: [footprint]
items.text:
At most one per file. Maps to the model's footprint facet (subject: Part).

Field Type Meaning library string A KiCad footprint library name name string The footprint's name within that library

Written into the KiCad netlist as library:name (design section 7). fransys_kicad writes this reference; it does not read the footprint itself.

items.title: [cable_product]
items.text:
At most one per file. Maps to the model's cable_product facet (subject: Part).

Field Type Meaning core_count integer The author's checksum: the lint's CABLE_CORE_COUNT compares it with core_colours. The model stores no count; it reads len(core_colours) (model-0082) core_colours array of strings One entry per core, in core index order, e.g. ["BN", "BK", "GY", "GNYE"]. Each is an IEC 60757 colour code: a base code, two base codes joined (GNYE), a base code with a number (BK1), or SH for a shield (model-0070); anything else is an ERROR gauge_mm2 string Cross-section in mm², read as Decimal shielded boolean pairs array of tables, optional One { cores = [a, b], screen = n } per twisted pair: two core numbers, and its SH core if it has one. The drawing labels the pairs P1, P2 (CC8)

CABLE_PAIR_INVALID (ERROR) refuses a core out of range or in two pairs. It also refuses a pair core that is SH, and a screen that is not SH or is named twice.

items.title: [function.protection]
items.text:
A protection function names its device in type: "fuse", "mcb", "motor_breaker", "overload" or "rcd". The loader writes it to FunctionTemplate.protection_type, null when absent. Lint: PROTECTION_WITHOUT_TYPE (WARNING), PROTECTION_TYPE_ON_NON_PROTECTION (ERROR), PROTECTION_LINK_KIND (ERROR, a switched link or a kind that does not fit the type) and SYMBOL_TYPE_MISMATCH (ERROR, a symbol of another type). A through link is protective for fuse, mcb, motor_breaker and rcd, and conductive for overload.

Default symbols (layout-0105). A symbol on the part or a layout choice always wins.

Function Symbol switch operated by push, open / closed at rest push-button / push-button-break switch operated by mushroom, closed at rest emergency-stop switch operated by turn, open / closed at rest selector-make / selector-break switch operated by position, open / closed at rest position-switch-make / position-switch-break switch, open at rest make-contact switch, closed at rest break-contact fuse fuse mcb, motor_breaker circuit-breaker overload thermal-overload, one box per pole rcd rcd protection with no type circuit-breaker

A switch is operated by its own part's operated_by, else by the nearest holder's (layout-0220, model-0222). An emergency stop states operated_by = "mushroom".

Poles (F4, model-0128). A pole is a switched or protective link, or a protection function's conductive link. Poles run in natural marking order, line side on top; no side fact keeps marking order.

The [function.connector] table is in part-file-connectors.md.

items.title: [function.plc_channel]
items.text:
A sub-table of the [[function]] entry it describes (P1): a multi-channel PLC module part has one [[function]], and one [function.plc_channel], per channel. Maps to the model's plc_channel facet (subject: FunctionTemplate).

[[function]]
name = "di_3"
kind = "plc_channel"
ports = [{ name = "3", role = "generic" }]

[function.plc_channel]
signal = "di"
channel = 3
Field Type Meaning signal string A SignalType value: "di", "do", "ai_current", "ai_voltage", "ao_current", "ao_voltage", "rtd", "relay" channel integer Channel number on the module

items.title: [rating], [function.rating] and [function.operating]
items.text:
[rating] (top level, at most one per file) is the part's own rating, e.g. a cable's rated voltage or a fuse link in its holder; it maps to the part_rating facet (subject: Part). [function.rating] and [function.operating] are sub-tables of a [[function]] entry (P1); they map to the rating and operating facets (subject: FunctionTemplate). power_loss_w is the heat given off at the rated load. resistance_ohm, nominal_power_w and nominal_current_a are stated at nominal_voltage_v. No check reads the first two (model-0125, parts-0009). A part states power_loss_w once, in [rating] or per function: both is POWER_LOSS_TWICE (ERROR). A function takes its template's rating, else its part's, as a whole record: a template rating with only an AC value hides the part's DC value (decisions model-0079, parts-0004).

[[function]]
name = "coil"
kind = "coil"
ports = [{ name = "A1", role = "generic" }, { name = "A2", role = "generic" }]

[function.rating]
voltage_ac_v = "250"
Table Fields, all optional [rating], [function.rating] voltage_ac_v, voltage_dc_v, current_ac_a, current_dc_a, min_breaking_current_a, power_loss_w, breaking_ac, breaking_dc [function.operating] voltage_ac_v, voltage_dc_v, nominal_voltage_v, max_voltage_v, min_voltage_v, capacity_ah, max_current_ac_a, max_current_dc_a, resistance_ohm, nominal_power_w, nominal_current_a, fault_current_ac_a, fault_current_dc_a, fault_time_constant_ms

A breaking list is non-empty. A breaking_dc point may add time_constant_ms:

breaking_dc = [{ voltage_v = "1000", current_a = "15000", time_constant_ms = "15" }]

min_breaking_current_a marks a partial-range fuse (an aBat link): the lowest current it breaks. It bounds no continuous current. max_current_ac_a and max_current_dc_a are a source's continuous current limit, charging included (decision model-0088).

Every value is a string in plain decimal notation (digits with an optional fraction), read as Decimal. A rating value is above 0; a [function.operating] value may also be 0 ("0", "0.0": a source's minimum voltage), decision parts-0006. A bare TOML float is FLOAT_FORBIDDEN and an integer is FIELD_TYPE. The lint refuses, as ERROR, a table with no field (RATING_TABLE_EMPTY) and a value outside those rules, negative or not plain (RATING_VALUE_INVALID). The RATING_VOLTAGE_BELOW_CIRCUIT and RATING_CURRENT_BELOW_BRANCH checks read a rating. Of the operating values, only max_current_*, nominal_current_a and fault_* are read. A part with no current rating limits no branch (model-0088).

items.title: [pcb]
items.text:
At most one per file. Maps to the model's pcb facet (subject: Part); marks a board part.

Field Type Meaning revision string

items.title: Rules
items.text:
• No floats. Every table is read with parse_float=Decimal. A bare TOML float (1.5 unquoted) is FLOAT_FORBIDDEN wherever it sits in the file; write it as a string ("1.5").
  • Quantities are strings read as Decimal. gauge_mm2 is the example.
  • Lengths are integer millimetres. A length field is a plain TOML integer.
  • The symbol key is a slug. symbol is lowercase and hyphenated ("operating-device", "change-over-contact"), naming a key in electrical-symbols. fransys_parts checks the slug's shape only; the layout engine reports an unknown symbol or unbound port.
  • symbol_port names a role of the symbol, not a marking of the part. The symbol knows shapes and calls its ports by role (in, out, com, nc, no); the part knows markings and calls the same ports by what is printed on it. ports.marking overrides what is printed (design section 6). A changeover binds by its throw roles.
  • Footprint is library:name. Never a bare name.
  • No multi-line strings. The loader finds a record's line by scanning the file text once for table headers (decision parts-0001); a multi-line string could hide a header. No string value may contain a line break (lint: MULTILINE_STRING, checked on the parsed values).
  • A file that cannot be read is a finding, not a crash. An unreadable or non-UTF-8 part file is FILE_UNREADABLE; lint and load_path still check every other file.

items.title: Worked examples
items.text: The demo part library, examples/demo-parts/, is the worked example of this contract and the fixture every test builds on. Its files are shown in the parts package README, packages/fransys-parts/README.md.

items.title: Packaging and pinning
items.text:
A part library is an ordinary Python data package: no build step beyond packaging the TOML files, no Fransys code inside it.

  • Normal use. A project pins the library as a git dependency with an exact revision: co-parts = { git = "https://...", rev = "<sha>" } in its pyproject.toml. uv.lock then pins the resolved commit, so a build needs no access to the library repository.
  • While authoring new parts. The project instead points [tool.uv.sources] at a local checkout (co-parts = { path = "../co-parts", editable = true }), so edits to a part file are picked up without a commit and a re-pin. This is switched back to the git form before the change ships.
  • fransys_parts.lint is meant to run in the library's own CI, so a bad part fails there and never reaches a project's build.

items.title: Versioning
items.text:
• schema (an integer, 1 today) is the part-file schema version, not the library's own version. A library can ship many releases against one schema.
  • A breaking change to this contract (a renamed field, a changed meaning, a removed table) bumps schema. It is never changed in place under the same number.
  • fransys_parts.SUPPORTED_SCHEMAS: frozenset[int] names the accepted schema values; today frozenset({1}). library.toml and every part file carry schema; a value outside SUPPORTED_SCHEMAS is the lint finding SCHEMA_UNSUPPORTED, naming the file and the value found, and a part file whose schema differs from its library.toml is SCHEMA_MIXED.
  • There is no migration framework. A library bumps schema for every part file in one commit.

items.title: Examples
items.text:
Whole designs from the examples repository, with their exports.

  • pump-station

items.title: pump-station
items.text:
A complete design built with Fransys from real catalogue parts: a pump cabinet and a relay interface board, released as two units, and the station that joins them. Every export Fransys produces for it is in out/.

Beta, like Fransys, until 1.0.0. Every drawing and list is also on the site: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/examples/pump-station/.

items.title: The station
items.text:
• A 400 V supply, a main switch, and two pumps. Each pump has a 4 A aM, 10x38 fuse, a Schneider LC1D09 contactor and a matching LRD08 overload relay. The main switch isolates, so the fuse has no switch-disconnector.
  • A 24 V DC control supply and a WAGO PFC200 controller (750-82xx) with 750 digital I/O modules. The 0 V of the 24 V supply is GND everywhere, and the PSU's DC output lands only on the rail terminals.
  • A relay interface board between the PLC outputs and the contactor coils: industrial 24 V DC PCB relays with no diode, since the PLC modules handle the coil. It is nested in the cabinet as a unit of its own.
  • Pilot lights, driven by an auxiliary contact on each contactor, and the field cables to the motors.
  • Every part file carries its datasheet rating.

items.title: What is here
items.text: Path What it holds build.py The design script. parts/ The part library: one TOML file per catalogue part. parts/README.md lists each with its datasheet. parts_typed.py The typed parts module, made by python -m fransys parts-module. out/ Every export: all/ for the station, cabinet/ for the cabinet unit, board/ for the relay board. Each folder keeps its CSV and XML files in data/. releases/ Frozen baselines of the two units. A test checks them with fr.verify. GAPS.md What this Fransys release cannot yet say about the station, and the workaround used. system.md, cabinet.md, relay-board.md The documents' cover pages.

items.title: Two levels in one script
items.text: build.py shows two ways to write a design. The easy level writes the incoming supply and the single circuits out, one device and one wire per line. The efficient level writes the two pumps as one pump() function called twice, takes their PLC channels from the PUMPS table, and uses the typed parts module.

items.title: Use it as a starting point
items.text:
This folder is a project of its own, set up the way your project would use Fransys: pyproject.toml pins Fransys at a release tag. Copy the folder, then:

uv sync
uv run python build.py             # rebuild out/
uv run python build.py --release   # write the unit baselines into releases/
just ci                            # lint, types and tests (needs just: https://just.systems)

items.title: Fransys
items.text:
Fransys is a Python toolkit for authoring electrical cabinet and harness designs and producing their schematics, parts lists and manufacturing exports from one model. This page lists every consumer task with its one spelling, then the install and the shape of a script.

Fransys is in Beta: the API may change between minor versions until 1.0.0, and each release's guide says what changed.

items.title: The public surface
items.text: The public surface has four parts: fr.__all__, fr.derive.__all__, fransys.colours, and every keyword of every public call and every d.* method, with the d.layout.profile keywords and the d.layout.sheet numbers. Nothing else is public, and every part has an entry in this guide.

items.title: Tiers
items.text:
Every fr.* function and handle method opens its docstring with one of four tier words.

  • Core: the calls a project is written with.
  • Detail: a call for a case no core call writes; its docstring names the core call to try first.
  • Read: reads a built model or a part library and changes nothing.
  • Output: builds, checks, reports, writes or releases.

A namespace sets the tier of the names under it, so they carry no word: d.* is core, d.detail.* and d.layout.* are detail, and fr.derive.* is read. Types, constants, colours and exceptions have no tier.

items.title: Which call first
items.text:
Write a design with the core calls below. They pair poles, take the next free terminal or core, and give layout the structure it draws. The detail calls in the table are for their cases only (detail.md).

  1. A cabinet or a board is a unit: @fr.unit, then d.add (units.md).
  2. Name places with d.location. Put each circuit in its own block, with d.function(tag, text):.
  3. Declare every supply with d.dc_supply or d.ac_supply. Start and end each path on its rails.
  4. Write each current path as one d.series(...), source first. Devices, functions, rails, strips, runs and cables are its elements.
  5. A branch between two neighbours is a d.parallel(...) element. A branch across several elements is a second series, from the split to the join.
  6. Pass a strip, a run or a cable to the series. It takes the next free terminal or core, on the right side.
  7. Bridge with bridged= on the strip or the run. Request a PLC signal on its function, K1.coil.plc(fr.DO, name), and pass the PLC module whole to the series: it takes its lowest free channel (authoring.md, how channels are numbered).
  8. A circuit that repeats is a Python function around these calls, fed by a table (examples.md).
  9. Add d.layout.* advice last, only where the structure leaves the drawing a choice.
detail call only for d.detail.wire(a, b, wire=...) two named pins off any path, such as a signal pair; one signal daisy-chained, d.detail.wire(a, b, c); a hop whose printed wire differs from its row X1[3], .inner, .outer a terminal whose number or side is fixed: a published pinout, or several wires on one terminal W1.core(BN, a, b) a core whose colour or number a termination plan fixes d.detail.net(name, *pins) a named net that no wire joins, such as a bus shown by its label d.detail.busbar(a, b), d.detail.rail_bond(a, b) a rack's internal jumper; terminals bonded through their rail

d.series raises has no pole pair: its part states no line side when a part does not say which pin is the line side. Fix the part file (side = "line", parts.md), or wire the pins with d.detail.wire. A real circuit that no core call can write is a gap in Fransys: report it with its smallest shape.

items.title: Install
items.text:
Fransys is not on PyPI yet. Pin it as a git dependency, at a release tag:

[project]
dependencies = [
    "fransys @ git+https://github.com/OleJBondahl/fransys@vX.Y.Z#subdirectory=packages/fransys",
]

Replace vX.Y.Z with the release you pin.

items.title: The shape of a build script
items.text:
A script starts a design from an installed part library (fr.design), authors it with d.device and wiring, adds a cabinet as a unit (@fr.unit, d.add), and passes the design to fr.build, which merges and freezes a model and lays out the schematic when a document keeps a SCHEMATIC page. fr.check collects every finding about the built model; fr.write writes the exports to a directory, raising instead of writing anything if check found an ERROR. A design with no document has nothing to draw, so build still succeeds and write still produces the parts-list exports.

from pathlib import Path
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Cabinet(NamedTuple):
    pass


@fr.unit("pump-cabinet", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="First", by="AB")
def cabinet(c):
    c.device("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5")
    return Cabinet()


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
d.add(cabinet, "U1")

result = fr.build(d)  # no document: no layout
print(fr.report(result))  # the summary, each error and warning with its fix, then the notes
findings = fr.check(result)
assert not [f for f in findings if f.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR]
fr.write(result, Path("out"))

fr.report(result) prints what the build found, so a script shows its warnings on every run.

items.title: Writing a project
items.text:
• parts.md: loading and linting a part library, the typed parts module, and a part's rating.
  • authoring.md: places, functions, devices, strips, bridges, supplies and channels.
  • series.md: series, branches, changeovers, cables, wire colours and earth pins.
  • units.md: a unit's boundary, its revisions, and nesting one unit inside another.
  • harnesses.md: adding a harness, and how its cables and plugs print.
  • documents.md: presets, covers, subjects, and one PDF per drawing.
  • build.md: build, check, write, release, verify, and where each can fail.
  • examples.md: worked examples, and a pointer to a full build script.
  • examples/demo-skid/skid.py, outside the guide: a whole skid cabinet on demo parts, as a worked design of high-level calls (its README says how to build it).

items.title: Detail and edge cases
items.text:
• detail.md: each d.detail call, W1.core, fixed terminals and d.layout advice, with the cases they are for.
  • drawing.md: what layout reads, a checklist for a readable cabinet, printed sizes and grid pitch.
  • layout-numbers.md: every d.layout.profile keyword and every d.layout.sheet number.
  • readability.md: fr.readability, the per-page and per-unit numbers behind the readability findings.

items.title: Reading a built model
items.text:
• reading.md: reading a built model back: tables, rows, designations and ratings.
  • reading-rows.md: the column constants, row types, row functions and printed texts of fr.derive.
  • reading-records.md: the record types, lookups and ratings of fr.derive.
  • overview.md: reading the system overview page write makes.

items.title: Findings
items.text: • findings.md: every finding code, what it means and the usual fix, on five pages by source: findings-validators.md, findings-render.md, findings-pdf.md, findings-kicad.md and findings-parts.md.

items.title: Reference
items.text:
• keywords.md: the signal types, handles, Severity and the keywords of the record constructors.
  • keywords-design.md, keywords-handles.md and keywords-output.md: one table for each public call, with each keyword's default, effect and an example.
  • kicad.md: importing a board netlist into KiCad, with the settings to use.

items.title: Moving from an older release
items.text:
• moving-to-0.20.md: the new fr.rebaseline call for baselines cut by an older release.
  • moving-to-0.19.md: the detail calls that moved to d.detail, and the rewrite from d.wire to d.series.
  • moving-to-0.16-and-0.17.md: what may newly stop a 0.15 or 0.16 build, the changed outputs and the new names.
  • moving-to-0.15.md: each renamed profile and readability name, the new releases= keyword and the system overview's Changes switch.
  • moving-to-0.14.md: every fr.derive name 0.14 removes, and what to use instead.
  • moving-to-0.6.md: each break from 0.5, with the old spelling, the new one and why.
  • moving-to-fransys.md: the alias, the pin line, the parts-module command and the intermediates folder for a 0.6.1 consumer of the old name.

items.title: For coding agents
items.text:
The official Fransys documentation is the site, one version per release. Read it there, never in the installed package folder (site-packages/fransys/). Paste this block into your project's CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md so every agent that works on the project finds it:

## Fransys documentation

- The official documentation is https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/ .
- Take the version from the installed package: `importlib.metadata.version("fransys")` is `X.Y.Z`.
- Start at https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/X.Y.Z/llms.txt. Its `llms-full.txt` is the whole guide in one file.
- Read a page as Markdown at its URL plus `index.md`, such as https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/X.Y.Z/guide/index.md.
- Import only `fransys`. Write with the calls the guide index names under "Which call first".
- Do not read `site-packages/fransys/`. Its guide is an offline fallback for when the site is unreachable.

The part-file format is in the part-file contract, at the same version path. For type checking a design script, read Type checking.

items.title: Offline fallback
items.text:
Without network access the guide ships inside the installed package. Find the version you have installed with importlib.metadata.version("fransys"). Find the guide folder with the standard resource-loading call for package data, in Python:

importlib.resources.files("fransys").joinpath("guide")

Read index.md next. This file restates no API. The guide pages and the package's own docstrings are the reference.

items.title: Authoring a design
items.text:
This page teaches how to write a design with fr.design: places, function blocks, devices, terminal strips, wires, cables, supplies, PLC requests and layout advice. Each task has one spelling, shown first written out and then with Python around it.

A Design is one object with no global state. Every call returns a handle, never a string, and later calls take it. A design is a draft: fr.build(d) freezes it (see build.md).

items.title: Easy and efficient
items.text:
Each task is shown twice and builds the same model both times. The easy level writes the circuit out, one device and one wire per line. The efficient level uses the same calls with Python around them: a loop over a table, a function for a circuit that repeats. Both use the same calls.

The pairs below are: a function block with devices, and a terminal strip with a series. The branched series pair is on series.md. The sections after them list the one-call tasks.

items.title: Name a place and a function block
items.text:
A place is where units and field devices stand: a room, a site, a ship's hold. d.location("HOLD", text) names it, and place="HOLD" on d.device or fr.design puts devices there. A cabinet is not a place. It is a unit that holds components, units and wires (see units.md). A function block is one circuit, such as one pump's or one string's: with d.function("LAMPS", text): puts every device made inside it in that block, and a circuit is never a place. Tags are bare: "HOLD", never "+HOLD", and a prefixed tag raises.

What place= changes, on every call that takes it.

value effect ... (the default) The item takes the design's place, the one fr.design(place=) named. With none named, it has no place. "HOLD" The item stands in that place. Its designation gains the prefix +HOLD, or +HOLD+BATT in a nested place. The place must exist. None The item has no place, even when the design names one.

A place sorts the lists by place and sets the + part of the printed designation. It does not move a cell on a drawing: d.layout.draw_in does.

d.device(tag, part, place=, parent=, mounted_on=, joins=, interface=, unused=, name=) adds one device. joins={1: K1.coil["A1"]} with parent=K1 fits a housing on K1's own leads: pin 1 is that pin, no wire. A contact block with parent= an operator head prints the head's tag, as -S1:11 (guide parts.md). part is a manufacturer part number such as "DEMO-LAMP-24".

Floating tags: every item call takes None for the tag and numbers the item from its class code. Pass name=, the identity a released number holds to; a floating call with no name= raises. An accessory takes its holder's designation, no number of its own.

external=True marks an item supplied by others. Every call that makes an item takes it: d.device, d.terminal_strip, d.cable and d.harness. The item has no BOM line. A strip's terminals are external with it; a cable's conductors carry no flag. Every drawing marks it: dashed boxes with "(by others)", dashed outlines round schematic symbols.

An external device or strip may take None for its part, when only its terminal names are known. It needs a tag. A part-less device names its pins with pins=. A part-less strip offers only .outer: see detail.md, "Equipment others supply".

# easy: function block
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24").output)
with d.function("RUN", "Pump run"):
    k1 = d.device("K1", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
    k2 = d.device("K2", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
    h1 = d.device("H1", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
    h2 = d.device("H2", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
    d.series(dc.plus, k1.aux, h1.lamp, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))
    d.series(dc.plus, k2.aux, h2.lamp, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))

# efficient: function block
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

LAMPS = {"H1": "K1", "H2": "K2"}  # lamp tag -> the contactor whose auxiliary contact lights it

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24").output)
with d.function("RUN", "Pump run"):
    for tag, contactor in LAMPS.items():
        k = d.device(contactor, "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
        lamp = d.device(tag, "DEMO-LAMP-24")
        d.series(dc.plus, k.aux, lamp.lamp, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))

getattr(dev, f"DI{n}") is the one spelling for a computed name. A name the device lacks raises an error that hasattr reads as absent.

A device with one function and a marked pin is read the short way: h1[1].

items.title: A place inside a place
items.text: d.location("BATT", text, within="HOLD") puts the place BATT inside HOLD, named by its tag. HOLD must exist already, or the call raises and lists the places. A device placed in BATT prints +HOLD+BATT. Without within= a place sits at the root.

items.title: Read a function or pin
items.text:
A device has functions, and a function has pins. Both are plain attributes and brackets.

Q1.coil is a function by name, Q1["A1"] a pin by marking, and Q1[2] a pin by number. A name or marking the part lacks raises and lists the choices. The vocabulary is the electrotechnical one: a make contact closes when its coil is on, a break contact opens, a line conductor is L1.

A printed marking that is not a Python name has two spellings. dev["XLA+"] reaches any pin by its printed marking. dev.XLA_plus reaches a function or a pin named XLA+: + gives _plus, - gives _minus, any other non-word character _, and a leading digit gets P_, so 24V+ is P_24V_plus and the pin 1/L1 is P_1_L1. getattr(dev, "24V+") reaches the raw name.

items.title: Strips and terminals
items.text:
d.terminal_strip("X1", part, count, description=, pe=) adds a terminal strip of count terminals, and X1[3] takes terminal 3. pe names the protective-earth part, and a run labelled exactly "PE" (X1.run("PE", 2)) takes it; without pe= that run raises. A terminal has two sides: wiring inside the unit reaches its inner side, a field cable its outer side. A wire or a series enters a strip at the right side without you saying so. A series that starts on a strip and goes on to a function leaves the strip on its inner side. One that goes on to a cable leaves it on the outer side.

With count, the strip makes all its terminals at once, so spares exist and count in the lists. A terminal joins the function block where it is first taken, and a spare joins the strip's own group. There is no group= keyword. A series picks the side itself. x1[1].outer is the field side, and W1.core(...) lands there. d.series(x1[3].outer, f1.element) pins the side. A series of only fixed terminals takes its width from the first; one terminal is one pole. A tuple takes one-terminal runs, (x4.l1[1], x4.l2[1]), and the colours of the net an earlier series made. interface= and unused= on d.terminal_strip mark terminals a unit boundary: True marks every terminal, and a tuple of numbers, interface=(1, 2), only those; the others stay inside the unit. On a run they take True only: x1.run("24V", 4, bridged=True, interface=True) (see units.md).

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 3)
h1 = d.device("H1", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
with d.function("FEED", "Lamp feed"):
    d.series(x1, h1.lamp, x1, wire=(BU, 0.75))

items.title: Bridges
items.text:
X1.run(label, n, bridged=True) takes n terminals as a named run, joined by jumpers when bridged=True. A run's bridged= bridges a named run, and a strip's bridges plain terminals. Two terminals are a run of two. Made inside a function block, a run puts all its terminals in that block. Made outside every block, it puts none: each terminal joins the block it is first wired in.

bridged=(first, last) bridges terminals first to last only, one jumper between each consecutive pair. A pair outside 1 to n, or with first >= last, raises and names the range.

A strip with a count bridges plain terminals with no run and no label: d.terminal_strip("X4", part, 6, bridged=(2, 6)) jumpers terminals 2 to 6, bridged=((2, 3), (5, 6)) makes two bridges, and bridged=True bridges them all. A bad range raises and names the fix.

X1.run(label, bridged=True) takes no size. The run grows as connections take its terminals, and each new one is bridged to the one before. feed[n] names a terminal already taken; a higher n raises. A strip or a run is also a core's end: each place takes its next free terminal, a series on the inner side and W1.core on the outer side.

# a growing bridged run fed by d.series
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24").output)
feed = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5").run("24V", bridged=True)
for tag in ("H1", "H2", "H3"):
    d.series(dc.plus, feed, d.device(tag, "DEMO-LAMP-24").lamp, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))

items.title: Wiring and cables
items.text: The series, branches, changeovers, cables, wire colours and earth pins are on series.md.

items.title: AC or DC supply and rails
items.text:
d.dc_supply(name, source) declares a DC supply from the L+ and L- pins of a device; its rails are dc.plus and dc.minus, and a series starts or ends on them. With no source device, such as a 24 V feed on terminals, give the pins and voltage=: d.dc_supply("24VDC", plus=X1[1], minus=X1[2], voltage=24). A source whose part states a nominal voltage takes no voltage=. mid= adds a middle conductor, as on a plus and minus 15 V supply.

Without mid, minus is 0 V and plus carries the voltage. With mid, mid is 0 V, plus is plus the voltage and minus is minus the voltage. names=(plus, minus, mid) renames the potentials; ac_supply takes one name per phase pin, then one for n.

earthing=fr.IT declares a floating supply; the default is fr.EARTHED. Two 0 V rails are two supplies.

fault_current_a= is the supply's prospective fault current in amps; dc_supply also takes fault_time_constant_ms=. A supply that states one is a source for the breaking-capacity check (reading.md). A dc_supply declared from a source device refuses both.

A nested unit's declaration of a supply name its container also declares is not a source.

d.ac_supply(name, voltage, *phases, n=None, names=None) declares an AC supply on one or three phase pins in phase order. Its rails are ac.L1, plus ac.L2 and ac.L3 for three phases. On three phases voltage is each phase's RMS to the star point: 230 for a 400 V supply. A pin's side and order on a rail come from the supply you declare. A rail draws its power symbol only when declared. A fused branch or a second source of one voltage is not a supply: make it a strip with a description, or wire it point to point. ac_supply on a fuse's pins raises "a fused branch is not a supply". A branch from the common feed is a second series; one looped at the line screws starts at its line pins (index.md).

import fransys as fr

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x0 = d.terminal_strip("X0", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 2)
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 3)
mains = d.ac_supply("230V", 230, x0[1], n=x0[2])
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", plus=x1[1], minus=x1[2], voltage=24)

items.title: Plug a connector
items.text: d.mate(a, b) plugs connector a into connector b, each a device with one function (units.md covers a mate across a unit boundary).

items.title: Add a harness
items.text: d.harness("W5") adds a harness item: see harnesses.md.

items.title: Request a PLC channel
items.text: K1.coil.plc(fr.DO, "Pump run") asks for a digital output named for the signal, and .scale("bar", raw=(0, 100), eng=("0", "10")) scales an analogue one. A series that ends or starts at a PLC module binds the request to a channel (next section). A request no series wires keeps the build's own allocation. d.rack("U1") adds the part-less rack the modules sit under with parent=; a d.harness rack stops with HARNESS_HOLDS_PLC_MODULE.

items.title: How channels are numbered
items.text:
A PLC module passed whole to d.series takes its lowest-numbered free channel, as a strip takes its next free terminal.

rule what happens Order A call takes the lowest free channel when it runs. Calls take channels in the order they run. Direction A module that ends a path gives an input. A module that starts a path gives an output. A module in the middle of a path raises. Kind The request on a function of the path, s1.no.plc(fr.DI, name), names the kind. With no request, the module's only kind for that direction. Two kinds and no request raises, naming both kinds and the request that settles it. Fixed a1.di_7 is a fixed channel, for one that an existing PLC program or IO list fixes. A fixed channel is taken, and the lowest-free rule skips it.

Sixteen sensors from a table in IO-list order get channels 1 to 16:

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24").output)
a1 = d.device("A1", "DEMO-PLC-DI-16")
io_list = [f"Sensor {n}" for n in range(1, 17)]  # the IO list, in channel order
for number, name in enumerate(io_list, start=1):
    sensor = d.device(f"S{number}", "DEMO-PB-NC")
    sensor.sw.plc(fr.DI, name)
    d.series(dc.plus, sensor.sw, a1, wire=(BU, 0.75))  # S1 takes -A1:1, S2 takes -A1:2, ...

To reproduce an existing channel map, write the paths in channel order. Use the fixed form for a channel that call order cannot reach, such as one after a gap. A program that reads channel 5 after channel 1 needs a1.di_5 for the second path. The paths after it continue from channel 2.

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24").output)
a1 = d.device("A1", "DEMO-PLC-DI-16")
start, reset, stop = (d.device(tag, "DEMO-PB-NC") for tag in ("S1", "S2", "S3"))
d.series(dc.plus, start.sw, a1, wire=(BU, 0.75))      # channel 1
d.series(dc.plus, reset.sw, a1.di_5, wire=(BU, 0.75))  # fixed: channel 5, after a gap
d.series(dc.plus, stop.sw, a1, wire=(BU, 0.75))       # channel 2: the lowest free one

items.title: Title block, revision
items.text: d.project(title=, number=, customer=, ...) fills the title block and d.revision(1, date=, text=) adds a history line. Both are optional.

items.title: Building a design
items.text:
fr.build, fr.check and fr.write are the three pipeline functions. build takes the design (and any documents), merges them into a model and runs the passes, the validators, and layout when there is a document. check collects every finding about a built model, including some build itself never sees. write writes the model's exports to a directory. It raises, and writes nothing, if any finding is an ERROR. check also places the system overview (overview.html) and returns its findings, so a whole-system or a unit write meets them at the same gate; build never does.

fr.__version__ gives the installed Fransys version. It is not in fr.__all__.

items.title: Where a build can fail
items.text:
Four stages. Each fails differently. A mistake in an authoring call itself, such as a design call the builder refuses, raises fr.AuthorError at that call, so a test catches it by name.

1. Loading a part library. fr.design(...) and fr.parts(...) lint every library they load and raise PartLibraryError if linting finds an ERROR. Nothing is built from a library that fails its own lint.

2. The build itself. fr.build(d, *documents) merges the design with the documents, then freezes the result into a Model. Two structural problems can raise here. build catches neither.

  • MergeConflict, when two records share one id with different content. This can even happen before build runs, at the second authoring call that creates the conflicting record.
  • FreezeError, when freezing finds one or more structural problems inside the merged records: a dangling reference, a bad value, or a missing required field. It aggregates every problem it found in .errors, not just the first, so an author fixes a batch in one pass.

The case a consumer meets is two instances of one unit release, same name and revision, authored with different content.

from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Io(NamedTuple):
    X1: fr.Device


@fr.unit("demo-io-board", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-09-27", text="First", by="OJB")
def board_a(d):
    return Io(d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True))


@fr.unit("demo-io-board", revision=1, interface_version=2, date="2026-09-27", text="First", by="OJB")
def board_b(d):
    return Io(d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True))


conflict_design = fr.design("demo_parts")
conflict_design.add(board_a, "U1")

try:
    conflict_design.add(board_b, "U2")
except fr.MergeConflict as e:
    assert "two different records share one id" in str(e)
    assert e.origin_a.file == e.origin_b.file
    assert e.origin_a.line != e.origin_b.line
else:
    raise AssertionError("expected MergeConflict")

Both functions declare the release demo-io-board, revision 1. The second gives a different interface, so it conflicts instead of deduplicating. e.origin_a and e.origin_b name the two call sites.

fr.build(d) always carries the part library the design was started from. Only the engine's own draft, d.draft(), leaves it out, and building that shows what a missing library does: every reference to a part is left dangling.

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x1 = d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P")

try:
    fr.build(d.draft())  # the authored records without the library
except fr.FreezeError as e:
    assert len(e.errors) == 4
else:
    raise AssertionError("expected FreezeError")

Four references are left dangling by the missing library: one RefError for each. e.errors holds all four, not just the first one freezing happened to find.

Any exception out of build other than these two is a Fransys bug, not something a normal script needs to guard against. Report it as a field case.

3. The validators. Every domain validator runs inside build, but an ERROR finding from one of them does not raise. It comes back in fr.check(result), and it also stops layout there: a model with a validator ERROR is returned numbered but unlaid, findings and all.

4. write. write computes fr.check(result) itself and raises BuildErrors if any finding in it is an ERROR, before touching out_dir. See below.

items.title: fr.check(result) is the one list of findings
items.text:
fr.check(result) returns every finding about a built model. That covers the PLC and numbering passes, the validators, layout, and the board check. When the model holds a document it adds the drawing and PDF checks. A script reads findings only through it.

The design above has one device and no wiring, so its document has nothing to draw. This one keeps only its schematic, the BOM page taken out:

from pathlib import Path

cabinet_cover = Path("cabinet.md")
cabinet_cover.write_text("# Cabinet\n")
doc = fr.document(
    fr.DocumentPreset.CABINET_SCHEMATIC, x1, cover=cabinet_cover, remove=(fr.PageKind.BOM,)
)

result = fr.build(d, doc)
assert len(fr.check(result)) == 4

fr.check(result) holds three DOCUMENT_EMPTY_LIST INFO findings and, most importantly, one ERROR, DOCUMENT_NO_DRAWINGS, that only the drawing and PDF checks find. A symbol with nothing connected is not drawn, so the schematic page has no drawing and the document no other page. A script that asserted the design clean would have shipped it.

write runs the same check internally, so it raises on those errors:

try:
    fr.write(result, Path("out"))
except fr.BuildErrors as e:
    assert len(e.findings) == 1
    assert all(f.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR for f in e.findings)
else:
    raise AssertionError("expected BuildErrors")

e.findings holds exactly the one ERROR, not every finding of fr.check(result). out_dir is left with nothing written for this build. No bad export, ever. There is no allow_errors, force or draft parameter on write, and none will be added.

items.title: fr.report(result) prints them for a person or an agent
items.text:
fr.report(result) returns one text of fr.check(result). Its first line counts the errors, warnings and notes. Each ERROR and WARNING follows with its message, one at: line per subject (the authoring call's file:line), its fix, and its row's URL on your version's findings page. The notes come last, counted per code on one line.

text = fr.report(result)
assert text.startswith("build: 1 error, 0 warnings, 3 notes\n")
assert "  see: https://olejbondahl.github.io/fransys/" in text
assert "/guide/findings-pdf/#document_no_drawings\n" in text
assert text.endswith("notes: DOCUMENT_EMPTY_LIST 3\n")

The fix and the URL come from the code's row in findings.md. Print the report on every build: a warning nobody reads is never fixed.

items.title: Which route carries which finding
items.text:
Each route below carries a different set of findings.

route carries when you read it result.findings What fr.build collected: the PLC and numbering passes, the validators and layout. After fr.build. fr.check(result) result.findings plus the KiCad, PDF and render checks, errors first. Any time after fr.build. fr.report(result) The text of fr.check(result), with each fix and the URL of its findings row. Any time after fr.build. fr.BuildErrors.findings The ERROR findings of the fr.write or fr.release run that raised. fr.release adds its release checks. When the call raises.

fr.build itself raises MergeConflict or FreezeError for a structural problem and returns no findings then.

items.title: No document, no layout
items.text:
Layout exists only to draw documents. A build with no Document draft skips layout entirely. There is no flag, and no other function to call.

result = fr.build(d)  # no document this time
codes = sorted(f.code for f in fr.check(result))
assert codes == []

written = fr.write(result, Path("out"))
assert sorted(p.relative_to("out").as_posix() for p in written) == [
    "data/bom.csv",
    "data/cables.csv",
    "data/cores.csv",
    "data/designations.csv",
    "data/plc.csv",
    "data/wires.csv",
    "overview.html",
]

fr.export_names(result, *, unit=None) gives the name write gives each export, by (kind, subject), without writing or compiling anything. A kind is bom, plc, wires, designations, overview, cables or cores (subject None); terminals, connectors or wago with the item's id; or pdf with the document's id. The key is a tuple: ("bom", None) for a whole-set file, ("pdf", <document id>) for a document. write names its files through it, so a script never builds a name itself.

names = fr.export_names(result)
assert names[("bom", None)] == "data/bom.csv"
assert [key for key in names if key[0] == "pdf"] == []  # no document: no ("pdf", id) key
assert sorted(names.values()) == sorted(p.relative_to("out").as_posix() for p in written)

With no document, check never runs the drawing or PDF checks: neither has a layout to read. write writes the same kind of file list as before, with no PDF, since a PDF comes only from a document.

items.title: Export file names
items.text:
Export names follow the rules below. One function builds every name, so a script never constructs its own. The v prefix is used only in file names, never in a title block or history table. The names are a built-in default with no option or template.

  • The set prefix. Every file belongs to one set: the unit written (unit=U) or the system (unit=None). The prefix is <set name>-v<V>.<R>, the set's name plus its version and revision in derive.revision_text's print form. A unit's name is its release name (demo-io-board-v1.1); the system's is the project's number (EX-1-v1.1). A system write of a model with no project record has no prefix: the system's own files keep their bare names (plain bom.csv), as the examples above wrote. A unit's document still takes its unit's prefix.
  • Prefix, kind, fragment. A name is <prefix>[-<kind>][-<fragment>].<ext>: demo-io-board-v1.1-bom.csv, per item demo-io-board-v1.1-terminals-X1.csv, and for the unit's own root the bare kind demo-io-board-v1.1-terminals.csv.
  • Where each list is. A unit's cables stay in the unit's own cables.csv, because a parent sees the unit as a black box.
  • A PDF is named by its subject, not its cover file. A document of the set itself is <prefix>.pdf; a harness_drawing adds -harness; a document of an item or location inside the set adds that subject's fragment. A document whose subject is a unit takes that unit's name in every write, a system write included, so out/all/ holds EX-1-v1.1.pdf beside cabinet-v2.1.pdf. Two instances of one release with a document each come to one name and raise a name-clash error; keep one document per release.
  • The data/ folder. Every CSV and XML export goes into <out_dir>/data/, changes.csv included; the PDFs, overview.html and changes.md stay in out_dir, so the files you open are not among the lists. The names are unchanged, and fr.export_names gives the path from out_dir (data/EX-1-v1.1-bom.csv).
  • Stale exports. write first deletes the set's old files in out_dir and data/. Those are the files whose names start with the set's name and -v, so a reused work folder keeps only the current ones. It also removes the flat CSV and XML files a write made before data/ existed. A system write also deletes the files that start with each unit release's name in the model and -v, for the unit documents. The old bare-name patterns are still cleaned for one more release. Known limit: a unit that leaves the model leaves its last PDF behind in out/all/.
  • Build times. result.times holds the CPU and wall seconds of each build step, and print(result.times) shows one line per step with its share of the CPU. With intermediates=, write also saves build-times.json there, the build steps then each output; out_dir never holds it.
  • Releases. fr.release writes the same paths, and its manifest lists them (data/...). A release stored before data/ keeps its flat paths in its own manifest and still verifies.
  • Changes in the overview. fr.write(result, out_dir, releases=into) takes the folder you pass to fr.release. When it holds a release of the system (the one at the model's revision, else the previous one), overview.html gains a Changes switch that marks what changed since it. Without releases, or with no release there, the page has no such switch.

Every file write writes is UTF-8 without a byte order mark, with \n line ends, on every OS.

items.title: No export ever carries an error
items.text: This is the point of the write example above. write computes fr.check(result) before writing anything. Any ERROR in it blocks every export into that out_dir, not just the one the error is about. A half-finished design still draws its schematic pages into intermediates, when given. out_dir only ever holds a design with zero ERROR findings.

items.title: Releasing a frozen baseline
items.text:
fr.release(result, into, *, unit=None) writes one unit's (or the whole system's) frozen baseline: its document set, as write would write it for that unit, plus a canonical listing, a manifest of file hashes and package/tool versions, and the model itself. The target is <into>/<unit release name>/<version>.<revision>/, or <into>/<project number>/<version>. <revision>/ for the system (unit=None). Every check runs first -- the same gate write uses, plus five checks of its own -- and any ERROR writes nothing, the same as write.

A unit's change list is relative to the unit, so a place that holds all of its items, added or removed, shows no change.

def board(revision, *, spare=None):
    """One unit design: the release `demo-io-board`, X1 on its boundary, X3, an optional spare."""

    @fr.unit(
        "demo-io-board", revision=revision, interface_version=1, date="2026-09-27", text=f"Revision {revision}", by="OJB"
    )
    def io_board(d):
        x1 = d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True)
        d.device("X3", "DEMO-CONN-2P")
        if spare:
            d.device(spare, "DEMO-CONN-2P")
        return Io(x1)

    release_design = fr.design("demo_parts")
    release_design.add(io_board, "U1")
    return release_design


release_result = fr.build(board(1))
release_errors = [f for f in fr.check(release_result) if f.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR]
assert release_errors == [], release_errors

target = fr.release(release_result, Path("releases"), unit="demo-io-board")
assert target == Path("releases") / "demo-io-board" / "1.1"
assert (target / "baseline" / "listing.json").exists()
assert (target / "baseline" / "manifest.json").exists()

# releasing the same, unchanged model again writes nothing new
same_target = fr.release(release_result, Path("releases"), unit="demo-io-board")
assert same_target == target

An unchanged release is a no-op: nothing is rebuilt, no file's timestamp changes. A released revision is frozen: releasing a unit again with different content raises BuildErrors naming REVISION_ALREADY_RELEASED instead of overwriting it (see findings-validators.md). The files are the consumer's -- commit them in your own repo, alongside the design script that produced them.

A container rebuilt against an old child release uses the child's old source from git. Fransys loads no frozen child. A history entry that names a revision never released is RELEASE_HISTORY_UNRELEASED; units.md has the rule.

items.title: Getting the change list
items.text:
fr.diff(result, into, *, unit=None, against=None) gives the Markdown change list from a stored release to the model as it stands now, without writing anything: use it while a revision is in progress. release() writes the same text into changes.md (and the same rows into data/changes.csv) once a previous release exists; the first release of a unit gets neither file. The revision text you author stays yours: changes.md is the evidence beside it, and nothing overwrites the history text.

second_result = fr.build(board(2, spare="X2"))
second_errors = [f for f in fr.check(second_result) if f.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR]
assert second_errors == [], second_errors

preview = fr.diff(second_result, Path("releases"), unit="demo-io-board")
assert "Added `-X2`" in preview

second_target = fr.release(second_result, Path("releases"), unit="demo-io-board")
assert (second_target / "changes.md").read_text(encoding="utf-8") == preview
assert (second_target / "data" / "changes.csv").exists()

against= names a released revision's folder ("1.1") to diff against. The default is the model's own current release if stored, else the previous released revision below it. fr.diff raises FileNotFoundError when it finds neither. A renamed item shows as one Renamed line; moving-to-0.20.md has the rule.

items.title: Checking a baseline stays true
items.text:
fr.verify(result, baselines) -> tuple[Finding, ...] reruns the same comparison release's own BASELINE_DIFFERS check does, for every unit instance the model has (and the system, when the model has a project) with a stored baseline. It writes nothing, and fr.write never calls it: run it where you want the check, most often a test that guards a released revision.

assert fr.verify(second_result, Path("releases")) == ()

third_result = fr.build(board(2, spare="X9"))  # X2, mistagged X9
third_errors = [f for f in fr.check(third_result) if f.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR]
assert third_errors == [], third_errors

findings = fr.verify(third_result, Path("releases"))
assert [f.code for f in findings] == ["BASELINE_DIFFERS"]

second_result is unchanged since its own release above, so verify gives nothing. third_result shares demo-io-board's revision 2 release identity but was never released itself, and its spare connector's tag differs from what 1.2 actually released, so verify catches the drift without anyone calling release again. A unit or the system with no stored baseline at all is not reported.

When a child moved release, BASELINE_DIFFERS names it right after units, as in demo-cabinet 1.1 differs from its released baseline in: units (demo-io-board revision 1.1 → 1.3). It names direct children only. A grandchild's move shows in its parent's own finding.

verify also re-hashes every file of every release under baselines, with no model needed. RELEASE_FILE_CHANGED means a listed file's bytes differ, the folder holds a file the manifest does not list, or the manifest does not parse. RELEASE_FILE_MISSING means a listed file, or the manifest, is gone. A text file (.csv, .json, .md, .xml, .html, .txt) whose bytes differ only by CRLF line ends passes, so a Windows checkout does not fail it. verify returns findings and blocks nothing.

After an upgrade that moved a printing rule, fr.verify gives BASELINE_RULES_MOVED (INFO) for each release cut by an older Fransys and fr.release refuses over one. Run fr.rebaseline(result, Path("releases")) once and commit the rewritten listing.json and manifest.json; the exports are untouched, and fr.verify is clean again.

found = fr.verify(second_result, Path("releases"))
if any(f.code in ("BASELINE_RULES_MOVED", "BASELINE_ROWS_UNCHECKED") for f in found):
    fr.rebaseline(second_result, Path("releases"))  # commit the rewritten baseline files
assert fr.verify(second_result, Path("releases")) == ()

items.title: Listing the releases
items.text:
fr.releases(root) -> tuple[Release, ...] reads every <name>/<version>.<revision>/ folder under root, in name, version and revision order. Versions and revisions sort as integers. A Release has name, version, revision, interface, listing_digest, nested, files and path. nested holds one ReleasePin (name, version, revision, listing_digest) per release nested in it. files holds (path, sha256) pairs. A folder with no manifest is listed with those fields empty. A manifest that does not parse raises ValueError naming its path.

Later Fransys versions may add manifest keys. They keep reading every manifest an earlier public Fransys wrote.

listed = fr.releases(Path("releases"))
assert [(r.name, r.version, r.revision) for r in listed] == [
    ("demo-io-board", 1, 1),
    ("demo-io-board", 1, 2),
]
assert listed[0].interface == "1"

# Which parents to bump: a release whose pin of a child is older than the child's latest release.
latest = {r.name: (r.version, r.revision) for r in listed}
stale = [
    (r.name, f"{r.version}.{r.revision}", pin.name)
    for r in listed
    for pin in r.nested
    if latest.get(pin.name) not in (None, (pin.version, pin.revision))
]
assert stale == []

The policy stays yours: tag names, who releases, which findings block and who gets a copy. A transmittal is a script over fr.releases that lists what went to whom. Fransys keeps no issue record.

items.title: Keeping designations fixed across revisions
items.text: fr.build(d, *documents, releases=None) takes a keyword-only releases, the same root fr.release writes into. Left at None (the default), numbering is free, exactly as above. Given the releases root, build reads each unit's own previously released numbering before assigning new tags: an item still in the same group keeps the number it was released with, and a number freed by a removed or moved item is never handed to a different item within that unit's version. A tag the engineer authors may still equal a pinned or reserved number by mistake; that is DESIGNATION_DUPLICATE (see findings-validators.md), not silently allowed. Releasing without releases= still catches a moved number, as DESIGNATION_MOVED.

items.title: Point a finding past a helper
items.text:
A finding names the file and line of the call that authored the thing. Set __tracebackhide__ = True in a helper that builds a repeated circuit, and the finding names the line that called the helper.

import fransys as fr


def lamp_pair(d, first, second):
    __tracebackhide__ = True
    return d.device(first, "DEMO-LAMP-24"), d.device(second, "DEMO-LAMP-24")


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
h1, h2 = lamp_pair(d, "H1", "H2")
result = fr.build(d)
assert fr.derive.item_designation(result.model, h1.id) == "H1"

items.title: Read a model id
items.text: Q1.id and Q1.coil.id give the model id of a device and a function. Read them after the build, as fr.derive.item_designation(result.model, Q1.id) does. Ids are for reading, never to wire.

items.title: Detail calls
items.text: Each call here is for a case no core call writes. Try the core call first (authoring.md): a series pairs poles and takes the next free terminal or core, and layout reads its structure. d.detail is a fr.Detail handle, as d.layout is a fr.Layout.

items.title: When a detail call is right
items.text:
call only for d.detail.wire(a, b, wire=...) two named pins off any path, such as a signal pair; one signal daisy-chained, d.detail.wire(a, b, c); a hop whose printed wire differs from its row d.detail.star(src, targets, wire=...) one point wired to many, one wire each; d.detail.wire(src, *targets) chains them instead X1[3], .inner, .outer a terminal whose number or side is fixed: a published pinout, or several wires on one terminal d.pair(a, w1, b) a signal pair through a cable, pin for pin, with no line or load side; it is a verb, not a detail W1.core(BN, a, b) a core whose colour or number a termination plan fixes d.detail.net(name, *pins) a named net that no wire joins, such as a bus shown by its label d.detail.busbar(a, b), d.detail.rail_bond(a, b) a rack's internal power jumper; terminals bonded through their mounting rail

A real circuit that no core call and no row here can write is a gap in Fransys. Report it with its smallest shape.

items.title: d.detail.wire
items.text: d.detail.wire(a, b, wire=(BU, 0.75), label=, n=) draws one wire. wire= takes the shapes d.series takes: a size, a table of rows or a (colour, size), but not a tuple per pole. A size or a table takes the row of the net. More than two pins draw a daisy chain, one wire per neighbouring pair. label="L1" prints a label on the wire. n=2 draws a second wire in parallel between the same two pins. A strip or a run as a pin stands for its next free terminal, on the inner side.

items.title: One point to many
items.text: d.detail.star(src, targets, wire=...) draws one wire from src to each target in the tuple or list targets, and none between targets. A strip as src stands for one terminal, shared by all targets. wire= reads as it does for d.detail.wire.

items.title: A wire with no row
items.text:
A bare number is always a size. A row's value in a table is a colour or a (colour, size), never a bare number. When d.series or d.detail.wire cannot give a wire its row as written, the row is read at build end from the rails its net carries. Only rails of the wire's own unit and the units below it count. A rail never crosses a unit boundary from its container.

A net that holds a PLC channel's signal takes DC_SIGNAL. A pin whose part states source_row (a drive's U, V and W) gives its row. A net with none of these is the error WIRE_ROW_UNRESOLVED, which names the net and the wire; give wire=(colour, size) on that series. A series of only cables, strips and loads needs no wire=.

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 4)
h1 = d.device("H1", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
h2 = d.device("H2", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
d.detail.wire(x1[1], h1[1], wire=(BU, 0.75), label="S1")
d.detail.wire(x1[1], h1[1], wire=(BU, 0.75), n=2)
d.detail.wire(x1[2], h1[2], h2[2], wire=(BU, 0.75))

items.title: Equipment others supply
items.text:
A part-less external strip offers only .outer. A field wire on it is a fixed terminal.

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BK

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x8 = d.terminal_strip("X8", None, 4, external=True)
q8 = d.device("Q8", None, external=True, pins=("L1", "L2", "L3", "N", "PE"))
d.ac_supply("S", 400, q8["L1"], q8["L2"], q8["L3"], n=q8["N"])
d.detail.wire(x8[1].outer, d.device("M1", "DEMO-MOTOR-4KW")["U"], wire=(BK, 1.5))

items.title: Fixed terminals
items.text:
X1[3] takes terminal 3 and .inner or .outer names its side. A series enters a strip at the right side by itself. .outer and .inner decide which column of the terminal CSV a wire lands in. Name a side only when the plan fixes it; d.series(x1[3].outer, f1.element) takes it too. A series may also start at a pin: d.series(k1.coil["A1"], a1.di_1).

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 3)
h1 = d.device("H1", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
with d.function("FEED", "Lamp feed"):
    d.detail.wire(x1[1], h1[1], wire=(BU, 0.75))
d.detail.wire(x1[2].outer, h1[2], wire=(BU, 0.75))

items.title: One wire to a PE terminal
items.text:
A cable's green-yellow core is the core way (series.md, Earth pins). A single wire is a detail.

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import GNYE

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", pe="DEMO-TB-PE-2.5")
pe = x1.run("PE", 2, bridged=True)
m1 = d.device("M1", "DEMO-MOTOR-4KW")
d.detail.wire(m1.motor["PE"], pe[1], wire=(GNYE, 2.5))
d.earth(m1.motor["PE"], pe[1])

items.title: A PE bar's screws
items.text:
A bar's function takes its next free screw (series.md, Earth pins). One wire to a screw is a detail.

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import GNYE

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
pe1 = d.device("PE1", "DEMO-PEBAR-20")
m1 = d.device("M1", "DEMO-MOTOR-4KW")
w2 = d.cable("W2", "DEMO-CBL-2X2X0.75-SP")
d.detail.wire(m1.motor["PE"], pe1.pe, wire=(GNYE, 2.5))  # screw 1
w2.core(5, pe1.pe)  # the one-ended screen, screw 2

items.title: d.detail.net, d.detail.busbar, d.detail.rail_bond
items.text:
d.detail.net(name, *pins, kind=) names a net of pins that no wire joins. kind is fr.CONTROL (the default), fr.SIGNAL or fr.GENERIC. It does not make a PE or supply net: those have d.earth and the supply calls.

d.detail.busbar(a, b) joins two pins by a rack's internal power jumper. d.detail.rail_bond(a, b) joins two terminals bonded through their mounting rail. Neither has a wire-list row, colour or gauge, and both close the net like a conductor.

import fransys as fr

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 4)
d.detail.net("BUS", x1[1], x1[2], kind=fr.SIGNAL)
d.detail.busbar(x1[3], x1[4])
d.detail.rail_bond(x1[1], x1[3])

items.title: W1.core
items.text:
W1.core(BN, a, b) wires one core between two pins, named by its colour or its number. The core colours come from the cable part. A green-yellow core goes to a protective-earth pin only.

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BK, BN, GY

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 8)
pe = d.terminal_strip("X2", "DEMO-TB-PE-2.5", 2)
h1 = d.device("H1", "DEMO-LAMP-24")
w1 = d.cable("W1", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5", length_m=5)
w1.core(BN, x1[1], h1[1])
w1.core(BK, x1[2], h1[2])
w1.spare(GY, at=x1[7])
w1.spare()
w2 = d.cable("W2", "DEMO-CBL-2X2X0.75-SP", length_m=25)
w2.core(1, x1[3], h1[1])
w2.core(5, pe[1])
w2.spare()

A core you leave unused is w1.spare(GY), or w1.spare() for every core not wired so far. at=x1[7] parks one on a pin. The cable drawing prints "spare" on its row. A screen (SH) earthed at one end takes one pin: w2.core(5, pe[1]). A part with pairs in its [cable_product] table gets a bracket and a P1, P2 label over each pair's rows.

fn.pins gives a function's pins as a tuple, in the order the connector list prints (1, 2, 10, A1). To land a cable's cores on two connectors pin by pin, loop over it. The pairing rule stays yours.

import fransys as fr

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
a = d.device("J1", "DEMO-CONN-4P")
b = d.device("J2", "DEMO-CONN-4P")
w3 = d.cable("W3", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5", length_m=2)
for core, (pin_a, pin_b) in enumerate(zip(a.x1.pins, b.x1.pins, strict=True), start=1):
    w3.core(core, pin_a, pin_b)

items.title: Worked example: star-delta winding ends
items.text:
A star-delta starter wires the six winding ends of a motor. The demo parts have no six-end motor, so a strip stands for its terminal box: X2 terminals 1 to 6 are U1, V1, W1, U2, V2, W2. K1 feeds U1, V1, W1 through a series. K3 joins U1-W2, V1-U2 and W1-V2. K2 shorts U2, V2, W2.

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BK

WIRE = (BK, 2.5)
d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x0 = d.terminal_strip("X0", "DEMO-TB-2.5")
ac = d.ac_supply("400V", 230, x0[1], x0[2], x0[3])
k1, k2, k3 = (d.device(tag, "DEMO-CTR-3P-24") for tag in ("K1", "K2", "K3"))
xm = d.terminal_strip("X2", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 6)
d.series(ac, k1.main, xm, wire=WIRE)
for pole, delta_load in enumerate((6, 4, 5)):  # K3 pole 1 joins U1-W2, 2 V1-U2, 3 W1-V2
    line, load = str(2 * pole + 1), str(2 * pole + 2)
    d.detail.wire(xm[pole + 1], k3.main[line], wire=WIRE)
    d.detail.wire(k3.main[load], xm[delta_load], wire=WIRE)
    d.detail.wire(xm[pole + 4], k2.main[line], wire=WIRE)
d.detail.wire(k2.main["2"], k2.main["4"], k2.main["6"], wire=WIRE)

The winding ends stay detail for two reasons. Each end is a fixed terminal, since the motor plate fixes which end is U2. The star bridge joins three load-side pins that no path pairs.

items.title: Reversing starter
items.text:
d.parallel of two contactors shares the poles in order, so it makes no phase swap. Until an option for a swap lands, write the reverse contactor's crossing with d.detail.wire: K2's line poles 2 and 3 take L3 and L2.

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BK

WIRE = (BK, 2.5)
d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x0 = d.terminal_strip("X0", "DEMO-TB-2.5")
ac = d.ac_supply("400V", 230, x0[1], x0[2], x0[3])
k1, k2 = (d.device(tag, "DEMO-CTR-3P-24") for tag in ("K1", "K2"))
xm = d.terminal_strip("X2", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 3)
d.series(ac, k1.main, xm, wire=WIRE)
for line, crossed in (("1", "1"), ("3", "5"), ("5", "3")):
    d.detail.wire(k1.main[line], k2.main[crossed], wire=WIRE)
for pole, terminal in enumerate((1, 2, 3)):
    d.detail.wire(k2.main[str(2 * pole + 2)], xm[terminal], wire=WIRE)

items.title: Flat wiring and fixed terminals on a page
items.text:
Two drawing effects need a detail call to show, and drawing.md states the rules. Point-to-point d.detail.wire hops with no declared supply give layout nets only: one large connected circuit piles onto a single page and overflows it (OUT_OF_CONTENT_BOX). Declare the supply and write each path as a series, and the same twelve relays spread over pages. A lamp wired from one fixed terminal of a shared run adds no marker, and neither does a terminal taken in each block.

from pathlib import Path
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU


class Cabinet(NamedTuple):
    pass


Path("cover.md").write_text("# Cabinet\n", encoding="utf-8")


def built(body):
    @fr.unit(
        "cab", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="First", by="XX",
        title="Cabinet", number="C-1",
    )
    def cabinet(c):
        body(c)
        return Cabinet()

    d = fr.design("demo_parts")
    d.add(cabinet, "U1")
    doc = fr.document(fr.DocumentPreset.CABINET_SCHEMATIC, "cab", cover=Path("cover.md"))
    return fr.build(d, doc)


def relays(c, declare):
    psu = c.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24")
    dc = c.dc_supply("24VDC", psu.output) if declare else None
    for i in range(1, 13):
        with c.function(f"F{i}", f"Relay {i}"):
            k = c.device(f"K{i}", "DEMO-RLY-2CO-24")
        if dc is not None:
            c.series(dc.plus, k.coil, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))
        else:
            c.detail.wire(psu.output["+"], k.coil["A1"], wire=(BU, 0.75))
            c.detail.wire(k.coil["A2"], psu.output["-"], wire=(BU, 0.75))


flat = {f.code for f in fr.check(built(lambda c: relays(c, declare=False)))}
declared = {f.code for f in fr.check(built(lambda c: relays(c, declare=True)))}
assert "OUT_OF_CONTENT_BOX" in flat
assert "OUT_OF_CONTENT_BOX" not in declared


def markers(own):
    """Count the link markers of 30 lamp blocks fed from one 24 V run."""

    def body(c):
        psu = c.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24")
        run = c.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5").run("24V", 40, bridged=True)
