items.title: Reading a model
items.text:
fransys.derive is the read side of a model: every designation, table, row and rating a script might need already has a function here, and layout, render and every output call the same ones. This page does not restate fr.derive's whole surface. Every function carries its own docstring at its definition, and that docstring is the full reference. What follows is a short tour of the read surface as this release documents it explicitly: enough to know what is there and how to reach for it.

Two facts hold across the whole surface, so they are said once, here:

  • Ids are opaque keys. A script looks a record up by its id (in a table, or by passing the id to a derive function); it never builds, parses or prints an id itself.
  • An item's name is item.key[-1]. There is no separate .name field.

items.title: The tables
items.text:
fransys.derive.units(model) returns every Unit of model, by id, as a frozendict[Id[Unit], Unit]. The other tables (nets, unit_releases, supply_systems, and more) follow the same shape: one function per record kind, keyed by id.

  • fransys.derive.nets(model): every Net of model, by id.
  • fransys.derive.unit_releases(model): every UnitRelease of model, by id. A UnitRelease is the product a Unit instantiates (its name, version, revision, interface, title and document number); several Units can share one release.
  • fransys.derive.supply_systems(model): every SupplySystem of model, by id. A SupplySystem is a declared supply and its rails (a potential name, its maximum voltage and, for AC, its phase).

items.title: One unit's release
items.text:
fransys.derive.unit_release(model, unit) reads the one UnitRelease record a Unit instance is of. It is the one reader of a unit's release facts.

fransys.derive.unit_location(model, unit) returns the location node unit is placed at: its root items' own location, or their nearest common ancestor; None when no root is placed.

fransys.derive.project_facts(model) returns the title block's six facts of the project, as (title, number, customer, revision, revision_date, author); all are empty with no Project.

fransys.derive.document_facts(model, document) takes the document id and returns the same six facts: a unit document's are its unit release's own, with customer empty and author the created of the unit's current revision. Any other document's are the project's.

items.title: Rails, boundaries and function kinds
items.text:
fransys.derive.port_rails(model, port) returns the rails a port carries, as a frozenset[str] of potential names: empty for a port that carries none, or is not in model. A rail only exists once some SupplySystem declares the potential and some Net carries it; wiring alone declares no rail.

fransys.derive.port_potential_rank(model, port) is the rank of the potential a pin carries, or None. A smaller rank is drawn higher up. It reads the supply's facts, never a rail's name. The order is AC phases, DC above 0 V, AC at 0 V, DC at 0 V, DC below 0 V, then PE. A pin behind a switch keeps its rail's rank. A pin reached from two rails takes the lower. fransys.derive.port_potential_current(model, port) gives the rail's Current, and None for PE or no rank.

fransys.derive.takes_energy(model, function) is True when function takes energy in: its part's declared energy when it has one, else True for a load, an actuator or a coil and False for any other kind. A box draws the pins of an energy-in function above those of an energy-out one.

fransys.derive.gives_energy(model, function) is True when function gives energy out: its part's declared energy when it has one, else True for a supply and False for any other kind. A box draws a function that takes or gives energy above a signal function.

fransys.derive.no_conductor_at(model, port) is True when no conductor (wire, jumper, cable core or link) ends at port. Unlike unconnected_ports, a mate or a declared net does not count.

fransys.derive.port_is_unused(model, port) is True when no conductor ends at port and no declared net has it. A mate does not count. fransys.derive.function_is_unused(model, function) is True when every port of function is unused: the function hide_unused_pins leaves off the page, and a contact among them is a spare in its coil's contact table.

fransys.derive.power_kind(model, net) returns a PowerKind for a declared net: SUPPLY, GROUND, PE or NONE. A net of class pe is PE. A potential of a DC supply is GROUND at 0 V and SUPPLY otherwise. An AC rail, a potential in no supply, no potential, or two potentials on one wired net is NONE. So is a wired net of exactly two ports. A point-to-point connection is a wire; only a net of three or more ports is a rail. A PE net stays PE. port_power_kind(model, port) gives the kind of a port's wired net. A DC supply declares its 0 V rail (rails={"24V": ("24", None), "0V": ("0", None)}). Without it, the 0 V net gets references, not a ground symbol. power_text(model, net) is the text a power symbol prints: the supply's name, else its potential. It is None for GROUND, PE and NONE. port_power_text(model, port) gives the text of the symbol at a port. is_rail_terminal(model, terminal) is true for a terminal on a DC rail or PE net, bridged to another terminal of its strip. A schematic page draws no rail terminal. A pin wired to one, or to another pin on a power net, draws the rail's power symbol. No wire joins two such pins. The terminal table and the wire list still hold every landing and wire. A terminal is drawn at the pin it serves, once per page. A single-wire contact, and a coil on a PLC output channel, are drawn at the pin they serve, with a reference back to their device. A rail symbol faces away from its box: up above a top pin, down below a bottom pin. A terminal with no wire on a page is not drawn there. One wired to nothing is only in the terminal list.

fransys.derive.wire_rows(model, *, unit=None) returns the wire list: one WireRow per wire, with from_, to, colour, cross_section_mm2 and label. The label is the two end designations joined by one space in a fixed order, the text the wire list and sleeves print. A schematic page prints no wire label. A jumper, a core, a link, a harness wire: none. fr.write writes these rows as <set>-wires.csv.

fransys.derive.boundary(model, unit) returns the functions that make up a unit's interface, as a tuple of function ids in id order. A function of any kind can be a unit's boundary.

fransys.derive.FunctionKind is the enum of what a Function exposes: COIL, CONTACT_NO, TERMINAL, CONNECTOR, SUPPLY, and so on. A function's kind is one of these.

fransys.derive.connector_facets(model) returns every connector facet, by the function template it describes, as a frozendict[Id[FunctionTemplate], ConnectorFacet].

items.title: Rows
items.text:
fransys.derive.bom_lines(model, scope=None, *, without=()) returns the parts list, one BomLine per installed, non-external part (by mpn, revision and part), or one line per nested unit when scope is a unit. scope narrows what is counted: None for the whole model, an item id for that item's subtree, an aspect-node id for what is placed there, a unit id for that unit's own items and its directly nested units, or fransys.derive.TOP_LEVEL for items with no unit plus one line per top-level unit. without= names items that an item, aspect-node or whole-model scope leaves out; a unit or TOP_LEVEL scope ignores it. TOP_LEVEL's type, fransys.derive.TopLevelScope, is exported only so a script can annotate a variable that holds it.

fransys.derive.NO_PLACE is the text "N/A" a coil's contact table prints after the mark of a contact that no conductor reaches, in place of a page position.

fransys.derive.bom_sort_key(model, item) is the sort key bom_lines orders a line's designations by: a terminal by its strip, group and index; any other item by its whole designation. Every list an engineer reads sorts through fransys.derive keys: designations in natural_key order, so -K2 sorts before -K10.

fransys.derive.is_cable(model, item) returns whether item is a cable: whether its part carries a cable_product facet (decision model-0108). fransys.derive.cable_items(model) returns every such item, as a frozenset[Id[Item]]. Neither reads item's own category or its cable facet, which records only the as-installed length. Every cable-selecting function on this page (harness_cables, top_level_cables, unit_cables, cable_list_rows) reads through one of these two, so none can disagree about what a cable is. unit_cable_page_key is gone: the block key is internal.

fransys.derive.reading_cables(model, unit) returns unit's cables, or the top-level ones.

fransys.derive.is_plc_module(model, item) returns whether item's part has category PLC_MODULE. A rack is an item with at least one such child, and plc_rack_modules lists them.

fransys.derive.plc_tables(model, unit=None) returns the PLC list as one PlcTable per controller or module, in the row order of plc_channel_rows. The PLC list has one row per pin, so a channel with two pins has two rows.

fransys.derive.unit_strips(model, unit) and fransys.derive.unit_boards(model, unit) return the terminal strips and the boards that unit owns directly, sorted by id, never those of a unit nested in it.

fransys.derive.mates(model) returns one MateRow per d.mate in the model, at every level: a mate on a board, and a plug mated to a unit's interface connector. A row holds the two mated functions (each a connector or terminal), a and b in the authored order, and a_designation and b_designation, the text the connector list prints. Rows sort by those two texts. Reach an item through the function. connector_rows covers board connectors only.

fransys.derive.terminal_items(model) returns every item that carries a terminal facet, as a frozenset[Id[Item]]. Select terminals through it, so no script rebuilds the set.

fransys.derive.pin_order(marking, port) returns the sort key of a pin: markings of decimal digits first by value, the rest after by string (1, 2, 10, A1). The connector list, harness_cables and the overview sort by it, and fn.pins follows it. Sort pins through it, so no script keeps a second order.

fransys.derive.harness_wires(model, harness) returns the WireRows of the wires on the harness's plugs.

fransys.derive.cable_list_rows(model, unit=None) returns one CableListRow per top-level cable, or per cable of unit, with its product facts. from_label is the first end's designation; to_label lists the others, in end order, joined by ,. An end on a device that prints its connectors as sub-parts names the connector behind the designation (+C1-A1-X1). pairs is the number of twisted pairs of the cable's product, None for a product without pairs, and fransys.derive.cores_text(core_count, pairs) is the Cores cell: 2x2 for two pairs, else the count.

items.title: Designations
items.text:
fransys.derive.item_designation(model, item) renders an item's own printed label, such as K1, or U1-K1 for one nested inside a board.

fransys.derive.port_designation(model, port) renders a port's label: the item's designation plus the port's name, dash-prefixed like every physical tag (-K1:13).

fransys.derive.reference_designation(model, item) renders an item's full reference: its location and its product designation together (+C1-K1).

fransys.derive.printed_designation(model, item) renders an item the way a list prints it: dash-prefixed, product part only, with no location segment.

Each of these takes further keyword-only options (an inner board to render relative to, a unit to render for that unit's own document); their docstrings cover the exact rules.

fransys.derive.item_label(model, item) takes the item's id and is item_designation's no-raise twin: an item's own text, or its authoring key joined by / when it has none yet.

fransys.derive.node_designation(model, node) renders a node's signed designation by aspect: +C1 for a location, =G1 for a group. It is the segment reference_designation prints for an item there. A title block's scope cell prints a location's full path, such as +R+S1.

fransys.derive.item_of_port(model, port) returns the item whose function owns port, the lookup port_designation itself reads through.

items.title: Ratings
items.text:
fransys.derive.part_rating(model, part) returns the rating stated on a part itself, for a part with no function to rate, such as a fuse link. None when the part states none. It reads the model after the build. d.rating and d.operating state a rating or an operating envelope while authoring; the functions below read it back.

fransys.derive.function_rating(model, function) returns the rating a function's template states, else its part's. None when neither states one.

fransys.derive.part_function_rows(model) returns one PartFunctionRow per function a part declares: its part, mpn, template, name, kind and rating, sorted by MPN. A part with no function, such as a fuse link, has one row with template and kind None and name empty. rating is the function's own, else the part's, the rule function_rating reads. It needs no design: a parts-only build is enough.

fransys.derive.function_operating(model, function) returns the operating envelope a function's template states. None with no template or no such facet.

fransys.derive.boundary_rating(model, boundary) returns the rating a unit states on one of its boundaries. None when the unit states none.

fransys.derive.boundary_operating(model, boundary) returns the operating envelope a unit states on one of its boundaries. None when the unit states none.

items.title: Checking a branch's current
items.text:
RATING_CURRENT_BELOW_BRANCH compares each rated function with the current its branch can carry. A branch is bounded by a full-range protective device's rated current and by a source's max_current_ac_a or max_current_dc_a. A partial-range fuse, one with a minimum breaking current, bounds nothing. A load's draw is not an input.

Every device on the branch must be rated at least the bound. Below it, the finding is an ERROR. Here a 160 A fuse protects a branch of a 186 A source, and the contactor pole is rated 150 A.

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BK

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
g1 = d.device("G1", "DEMO-STRING-864V")
f1 = d.device("F1", "DEMO-FUSE-DC-160")
k1 = d.device("K1", "DEMO-CONTACTOR-DC")
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 2, external=True)
dc = d.dc_supply("HV", g1.string)
d.series(dc.plus, f1, k1, x1, wire=(BK, 1.5))
d.series(dc.minus, x1, wire=(BK, 1.5))

result = fr.build(d)
(finding,) = [f for f in fr.check(result) if f.code == "RATING_CURRENT_BELOW_BRANCH"]
assert finding.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR

fr.derive.current_chains(model) returns the rated paths, grouped by loop, in order from the supply end. Each position names its functions and its bounds. A bound holds the value, the function that set it and its role, source or protection. Here the fuse's 160 A is the smallest limit reaching the pole.

bounds = {b for c in fr.derive.current_chains(result.model) for p in c.positions for b in p.bounds}
assert {(b.value, b.role.value) for b in bounds} == {(160, "protection")}

Not checked: isolation, a cable against its installation, busbar authoring, a through-hole sensor, and per-path ratings across the functions of one part. A rated busbar item is checked like any other device.

items.title: Checking a fault and a load
items.text:
RATING_BREAKING_BELOW_FAULT compares a protective device's breaking points with the prospective fault current at its position. fr.derive.prospective_fault(model) returns what it reads: one ProspectiveFault per protective position and current kind. An entry holds the position, the kind, current_a, time_constant_ms, the source functions counted and the declared supplies counted.

A source is a function that gives energy, or a supply declared by pins that states fault_current_a. A supply input takes energy and is no source. A source function with more than two conductive ports counts as no source: its pins would have to be grouped by rail.

A bolted fault at one terminal of the device joins it to every other rail of the supplies the device reaches. A DC fuse behind a power supply does not see the AC rails. The device carries the sources on a path from the fault to its other terminal. A series run of sources counts at its largest member and parallel runs add. The larger of the two terminals' values is the entry's.

The value is conservative only given every feed declared. Cable and busbar resistance are ignored, which errs high. An undeclared feed counts as no source, which errs low, so declare every feed's fault current. A position no source reaches reads 0. A counted source that states none makes the value None, and the check stays silent.

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BK

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 4)
f1 = d.device("F1", "DEMO-FUSE-DC-160")
dc = d.dc_supply("HV", plus=x1[1], minus=x1[2], voltage=24, fault_current_a=6000)
d.series(dc.plus, f1.element, x1, wire=(BK, 1.5))
d.series(dc.minus, x1, wire=(BK, 1.5))

(fault,) = fr.derive.prospective_fault(fr.build(d).model)
assert fault.current_a == 6000
assert fault.time_constant_ms is None

LOAD_ABOVE_LIMIT and LOADS_ABOVE_LIMIT compare a load's draw with the limit that bounds it. fr.derive.load_limits(model) returns one LoadLimit per load edge: the function, the port of a star edge (None for a two-port load), the kind, draw_a and the bound. The bound is a CurrentBound, or None when no limit bounds the load. The draw is the part's nominal_current_a, as stated.

items.title: A worked example
items.text:
The design is authored with fr.design; every read below runs on result.model after the build. A pin handle such as housing[1] has an .id; an item is found by its tag in fr.derive.items(model).

from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BN


class Io(NamedTuple):
    P1: fr.Device


@fr.unit("power-tap", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-09-26", text="First", by="XX")
def power_tap(u):
    return Io(u.device("P1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True))


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
housing = d.device("X10", "DEMO-CONN-2P")
loose = d.device("X11", "DEMO-CONN-2P")
cable = d.cable("W1", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5", length_m=2)
cable.core(BN, housing[1], loose[1])
d.mate(housing, loose)

supply = d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24")
dc = d.dc_supply("main", supply)
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 1)
d.series(dc.plus, x1, wire=(BN, 0.75))
d.add(power_tap, "U1")

result = fr.build(d)  # no document: no layout
model = result.model
ids = {item.tag: item.id for item in fr.derive.items(model).values() if item.tag}

(unit_id,) = fr.derive.units(model)
release = fr.derive.unit_release(model, unit_id)
assert release.name == "power-tap"

(boundary_function,) = fr.derive.boundary(model, unit_id)
assert fr.derive.functions(model)[boundary_function].kind is fr.derive.FunctionKind.CONNECTOR

assert fr.derive.port_rails(model, x1[1].inner.id) == frozenset({"24V"})
assert fr.derive.nets(model)
assert len(fr.derive.bom_lines(model)) == 4  # connector, cable, supply, terminal
assert len(fr.derive.cable_list_rows(model)) == 1
assert len(fr.derive.contents_rows(fr.derive.top_level_cables(model))) == 1
assert fr.derive.printed_designation(model, ids["X11"]) == "-X11"
(mate,) = fr.derive.mates(model)
assert (mate.a_designation, mate.b_designation) == ("-X10", "-X11")

cable_part = fr.derive.items(model)[ids["W1"]].part
assert cable_part is not None
cable_rating = fr.derive.part_rating(model, cable_part)
assert cable_rating is not None and cable_rating.voltage_ac_v == 500

items.title: Wiring a design
items.text: This page teaches how to wire a design: d.series along a current path, branches and changeovers, cables, wire colours and earth pins. It follows authoring.md, which holds the places, devices and strips these calls join.

items.title: Wiring and cables
items.text: d.series takes wire= in four shapes (Wire colours): a colour code and a cross-section in mm2, a size, a table of rows, or a tuple of (colour, mm2), one per pole.

items.title: Wire along a current path
items.text: d.series(a, b, c, wire=(BU, 0.75)) wires elements end to end: each one's load side to the next one's line side, one wire per pole. A supply rail, a run, a device function, a cable and a strip are all elements. A function is a series element when its part names its line side; else the series raises and names it. A part-less external device may end a series: its pins meet the poles in declared order; anywhere else it raises.

items.title: Branch inside a series
items.text:
d.parallel(a, b) is an element of a series: each member sits between the previous load and the next line.

A branch across several elements is a second series, from the split to the join. Below, the second series wires S1:NC to K3, K3 to K4 and K4 to the coil K2:A1 in WH 0.5.

# easy: a branch across several elements
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU, WH

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
psu = d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", psu.output)
s1 = d.device("S1", "DEMO-CTR-BLOCK-1NO1NC")
s2 = d.device("S2", "DEMO-CTR-BLOCK-1NO1NC")
k2 = d.device("K2", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
k3 = d.device("K3", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
k4 = d.device("K4", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
d.series(dc.plus, s1.nc, s2.no, k2.coil, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))
d.series(s1.nc, k3.aux, k4.aux, k2.coil, wire=(WH, 0.5))

# efficient: a branch across several elements
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU, WH

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
psu = d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", psu.output)
s1, s2 = (d.device(tag, "DEMO-CTR-BLOCK-1NO1NC") for tag in ("S1", "S2"))
k2, k3, k4 = (d.device(tag, "DEMO-CTR-3P-24") for tag in ("K2", "K3", "K4"))
d.series(dc.plus, s1.nc, s2.no, k2.coil, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))
d.series(s1.nc, *(k.aux for k in (k3, k4)), k2.coil, wire=(WH, 0.5))

items.title: A changeover in a series
items.text:
k1.co_1.no and k1.co_1.nc are the two throws of a changeover, each a series element: line at the common, load at the throw. The first series that reaches the common wires it once, for both series. Passing the whole changeover raises: a changeover is two throws, so use K1.co_1.no or K1.co_1.nc. Between two fixed terminals a throw is entered and the common leaves: d.series(x6[2], k1.co_1.no, x7[2]). After a supply the common is wired to the supply's poles.

import fransys as fr

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24"))
k1 = d.device("K1", "DEMO-RLY-2CO-24")
k2 = d.device("K2", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
k3 = d.device("K3", "DEMO-RLY-2CO-24")
d.series(dc.plus, k1.co_1.no, k2.coil, dc.minus, wire=0.75)
d.series(k1.co_1.nc, k3.coil, dc.minus, wire=0.75)

A selector part has its throws on the line side. The series enters it at its throws and draws it turned.

items.title: Contacts that switch together
items.text:
d.poles(k1.co_1, k1.co_2, k1.co_3) groups one-pole contacts of one device, in pole order, as one element. It draws as one multi-pole symbol, and each contact keeps its place in the coil's table. A changeover group gives .no and .nc. selector=True turns its throws to the line, here selecting supply A or B for M1:

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
xa, xb = d.terminal_strip("XA", "DEMO-TB-2.5"), d.terminal_strip("XB", "DEMO-TB-2.5")
a = d.ac_supply("A", "230", xa[1], xa[2], xa[3], names=("A_L1", "A_L2", "A_L3"))
b = d.ac_supply("B", "230", xb[1], xb[2], xb[3], names=("B_L1", "B_L2", "B_L3"))
qa, qb = d.device("QA", "DEMO-MCB-3P"), d.device("QB", "DEMO-MCB-3P")
k1, m1 = d.device("K1", "DEMO-RLY-4CO-24"), d.device("M1", "DEMO-MOTOR-4KW")
q = d.poles(k1.co_1, k1.co_2, k1.co_3, selector=True)
d.series(a, qa.element, q.no, m1, wire=2.5)
d.series(b, qb.element, q.nc, wire=2.5)

The pair below feeds a coil from a supply through a bridged run.

# easy: terminal strip and series
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
psu = d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", psu.output)
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5")
feed = x1.run("coil supply", 3, bridged=True)
k1 = d.device("K1", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
k2 = d.device("K2", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
d.series(dc.plus, feed, k1.coil, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))
d.series(dc.plus, feed, k2.coil, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))

# efficient: terminal strip and series
import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
psu = d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", psu.output)
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5")
feed = x1.run("coil supply", 3, bridged=True)


def feed_coil(tag: str) -> None:
    coil = d.device(tag, "DEMO-CTR-3P-24").coil
    d.series(dc.plus, feed, coil, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))


for tag in ("K1", "K2"):
    feed_coil(tag)

items.title: How a series pairs
items.text:
A series wires each element's load poles to the next element's line poles. The rule:

  • Poles pair by conductor mark (L1, L2, L3, N) when every end has one, else in order.
  • A function is an element when its part names its line side (side = "line", parts.md).
  • A strip or a cable takes the next free terminal or core, on the side the path enters.
  • A path from a supply with n= joins N only where an element has a pole for it. A path of three poles from a three-phase supply leaves N unwired.
  • Connectors pair their pins in pin order when they are a series' two ends.
  • A tuple of one device's pins, (s1.x1[1], s1.x1[4]), is an element, first or last only; the written order is the pole order. Fn.pins lists them. A one-pole function and a pin make a two-wide end the same way: (q1.pole_1, n1.N). A terminal slice has .outer and .inner as one terminal has: x1[1:4].outer.

A refusal starts with one of these texts. Each has one fix.

refusal starts fix <fn> has no line/load pole pair a bare function end never pairs its pins by position: pass <fn>.pins (or a slice), or d.detail.wire <device> has no function of N poles pass the function, such as K1.main, not the device <device>: a and b both have poles, say which pass the function you mean N poles into M: name the pins pass elements with equal pole counts conductors L1, L2 into L1, L3: name the pins pass elements whose conductor marks agree <element> has N poles; a path from S takes pass the supply's phases, or the phases and N row <row> value <n> is a bare number, a size give the colour and the size as a tuple, such as ("BK", 1.5) a pin or a tuple of pins stands only put it first or last; else d.detail.wire a changeover is two throws pass K1.co_1.no or K1.co_1.nc a cable sits between two elements that are not cables put a plain element on each side of the cable <run a> and <run b> both take poles, <run> takes poles a bridged run in a series, alone or in a parallel, shorts its poles: give each pole its own sized run and take (x1.run("L1", n, bridged=True)[1], ...) as a tuple, one terminal per pole

items.title: Cables
items.text:
d.cable("W1", part, length_m=) adds a cable. Pass it to a series between two elements: each path takes the next free core, coloured by the cable part, and needs no wire=. parent=W5 puts the cable in harness W5, as on d.device.

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BU

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24").output)
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 4)
w1 = d.cable("W1", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5", length_m=5)
d.series(dc.plus, x1, w1, d.device("H1", "DEMO-LAMP-24").lamp, dc.minus, wire=(BU, 0.75))

A core with a fixed colour or number is W1.core(BN, a, b): see detail.md. Use d.pair(x8[1:3], w1, b1.sig) rather than d.series when the ends state no line or load side: core i joins pin i to pin i.

items.title: Wire colours
items.text: A colour is an IEC 60757 code imported from fransys.colours: BK, BN, RD, OG, YE, GN, BU, VT, GY, WH, PK, GD, SR, TQ, and the two-colour GNYE. Write wire=(BU, 0.75) for a blue 0.75 mm2 wire.

items.title: Colour by what a wire carries
items.text:
A design has nine wire rows: fr.DC_SUPPLY, fr.DC_GROUND, fr.DC_CONTROL, fr.DC_SIGNAL, fr.AC_L1, fr.AC_L2, fr.AC_L3, fr.AC_N and fr.AC_CONTROL. A row's value is a colour, or a colour and a size. d.series picks each wire's row from what it carries.

fr.design(library, wiring={row: value}) sets rows for the design. @fr.unit(..., wiring={row: value}) sets rows for that unit's body. A unit never inherits its parent's rows. With no wiring= it draws the IEC 60204-1 default: AC phases BK, AC_N BU, AC_CONTROL RD, every DC row BU, no sizes.

d.series(..., wire=) takes three shapes:

  • a size, wire=0.75: every wire takes its row's colour at that size.
  • a table, wire={fr.DC_CONTROL: (WH, 0.75)}: replaces only those rows for this series.
  • a spec, wire=(BU, 0.75): every wire gets that colour and size, and the rows are ignored.

A wire whose row has no size and no size on the series is WIRE_ROW_UNRESOLVED.

A series that starts on one rail (dc.plus, ac.L1) is a control path. A wire at the rail's potential takes the rail's row. A fuse or a contact ends that potential: the wires after it take DC_CONTROL or AC_CONTROL. A series that starts on a whole supply (dc, ac) is a power path: each pole keeps its conductor's row through every element. On a supply with n=, the first element with poles decides: as many as the phases leaves N unwired, one more takes N. A series that starts on no rail takes the rows the earlier series gave its net.

A wire with no row when written is resolved at build end (d.detail page, "A wire with no row").

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import BK, RD, WH

d = fr.design("demo_parts", wiring={
    fr.DC_SUPPLY: RD, fr.DC_CONTROL: WH, fr.DC_GROUND: BK,
})
dc = d.dc_supply("24VDC", d.device("G1", "DEMO-PSU-24"))
s1 = d.device("S1", "DEMO-CTR-BLOCK-1NO1NC")
k1 = d.device("K1", "DEMO-CTR-3P-24")
d.series(dc.plus, s1.no, k1.coil, dc.minus, wire=0.75)  # RD, WH, BK, each 0.75 mm2

items.title: Earth pins
items.text:
d.earth(*pins) declares the PE net; a wire to the PE terminal builds it. A unit has one PE net: each further d.earth call in it adds its pins to that net. Call d.earth before draft(); a later call raises. Every pin joined by d.earth draws the PE symbol, wired or not. A wire to a PE terminal adds its list row. A series through a cable lands its GNYE core on the load's PE port and the strip's next free PE terminal, else open and earthed. With no PE end and more poles than non-earth cores, the series raises an error. It names the cable and both counts; pick a cable with that many non-earth cores. A load with no PE port leaves the far end open, the near end on the strip's PE terminal. A single wire to a PE terminal is d.detail.wire: see detail.md.

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import GNYE

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", pe="DEMO-TB-PE-2.5")
pe = x1.run("PE", 2, bridged=True)
m1 = d.device("M1", "DEMO-MOTOR-4KW")
w1 = d.cable("W1", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5", length_m=3)
w1.core(GNYE, m1.motor["PE"], pe[1])
d.earth(m1.motor["PE"], pe[1])

A PE bar takes its landings. Pass the bar's function where a pin goes: it takes its next free screw and joins it to the PE net. A bar with every screw taken raises. A bar cut to length from stock writes no port, so each landing makes a screw. The bar is never drawn; each end on it draws the PE symbol. A cable core lands on a screw as on any pin; a single wire is d.detail.wire: see detail.md.

import fransys as fr
from fransys.colours import GNYE

d = fr.design("demo_parts")
pe1 = d.device("PE1", "DEMO-PEBAR-20")
m1 = d.device("M1", "DEMO-MOTOR-4KW")
w1 = d.cable("W1", "DEMO-CBL-4G1.5", length_m=3)
w2 = d.cable("W2", "DEMO-CBL-2X2X0.75-SP")
w1.core(GNYE, m1.motor["PE"], pe1.pe)  # screw 1
w2.core(5, pe1.pe)  # the one-ended screen, screw 2

items.title: Units
items.text:
A unit is a released, independently built part of a design: a board, a cabinet, a box, anything built and delivered on its own revision. This page shows how to write one, mark its interface, record its revisions and nest it in a cabinet. A cabinet is itself a unit: it holds components, units and wires, and it is never split into places.

@fr.unit(name, revision=, interface_version=, date=, text=, by=) turns a Python function into a unit. The function builds the unit's devices on the design it receives and returns an instance of a typing.NamedTuple class, one field per interface device. d.add(fn, "U1") builds the unit into your design as instance U1 and returns it, typed. Any other return raises. Every device the function creates belongs to that unit. @fr.unit(..., wiring={row: value}) sets the unit's wire rows (series.md, Wire colours). With no wiring= the unit draws the IEC default, never its parent's rows.

The second argument is the instance's printed tag, bare and with no lowercase letter: "U3", never "u3" or "-U3". It is also the instance's key. A container prints the tag before the unit's own designation, so a connector J1 of instance U3 prints -U3-J1. The unit's own document is unchanged. None floats the number: d.add(fn, None, name="module1") takes the next free number of the unit's class code, set with class_code="U" on @fr.unit (or by the part file's). name= is the identity a released number holds to. A floating add with no name= or no class code raises.

name is a key, not a designation: write demo-io-board, never -demo-io-board. A prefix raises an error. version= (default 1), title= and number= are the unit's own title-block fields. An empty title or number gives a TITLE_BLOCK_UNIT_IDENTITY_MISSING warning on the unit's own document.

revision and interface_version are numbers you bump by hand. Revisions count within one version: a unit's first version runs 1.1, 1.2, and so on, and its second version starts again at 2.1. interface_version is the unit's boundary version.

items.title: The interface
items.text:
d.device(tag, part, interface=True) marks a device as part of the unit's interface: the point a container may reach into the unit through. Any function may be an interface: a connector, a terminal, a PLC channel, a coil or a supply output. A cable landing straight on a channel, with no strip between, is the use. interface=True marks every function of the device; interface=("coil",) names some, and the others stay inside the unit.

On a terminal strip interface=(1, 2) names terminals by number and unused= works the same; True marks every terminal. A run takes interface=True or unused=True for the whole run. A container reaches only the boundary terminals, and d.add(..., unused=("X1",)) covers only those.

d.device(tag, part, unused=True) declares an interface device left unconnected on purpose, so the build does not ask for it to be wired. unused=True on a device that is not an interface marks it as one too. The tuple the function returns names the devices a container can reach: io.X1 is the field X1. A misspelt field is a type-checker error. A field may hold a nested unit's interface field. That connector, strip, run or terminal becomes this unit's interface too, one level at a time, and prints its full path. The black box a page draws for a nested unit is the unit directly in the page's unit that holds it. A field that holds a strip, a run or a terminal is typed fr.TerminalStrip, fr.Run or fr.Terminal. d.series and d.detail.wire from a container reach the unit strip's free boundary terminals, the PE core the unit's PE run, and never add one. Carry a strip or a run in the interface when a container wires several terminals in one series, as io.x5[1:5]. Separate fr.Terminal fields cannot be sliced.

A device with several functions takes the names of the boundary ones: interface=("x1",), unused=("x2",). True takes every function. A name the part lacks raises and lists its functions; a part class from fr.parts rejects it when the type checker runs.

X1.x1.limits(rating=, operating=) states the values the unit promises on one boundary function. Read them from a part with d.rating(part, fn) and d.operating(part, fn). It does not mark the boundary: interface=True on the device does. Calling it with no value raises. X1[1].limits(rating=, operating=) does the same for a terminal's boundary, with the same refusals.

from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Feed(NamedTuple):
    X1: fr.TerminalStrip


@fr.unit("demo-supply-strip", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def supply_strip(d):
    x1 = d.terminal_strip("X1", "DEMO-TB-2.5", 2, interface=True)
    x1[1].limits(rating=d.rating("DEMO-PSU-24", "input"))
    return Feed(x1)

import subprocess
import sys
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr

subprocess.run(
    [sys.executable, "-m", "fransys", "parts-module", "demo_parts", "demo_typed.py"], check=True
)
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import demo_typed as P


class Io(NamedTuple):
    X1: P.DEMO_CONN_2P


@fr.unit("demo-supply-box", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def box(d: fr.Design) -> Io:
    x1 = d.device("X1", P.DEMO_CONN_2P, interface=True)
    x1.x1.limits(rating=d.rating("DEMO-PSU-24", "input"))
    return Io(x1)

Annotate each device field with the generated part class it was built from, as P.DEMO_CONN_2P above. A bare fr.Device hides the part's functions from the type checker. A unit may also hand back a value beside its devices. Annotate that field with its fr.derive type, for example fr.derive.Operating, with | None where a read may find nothing.

class Supply(NamedTuple):
    X1: P.DEMO_CONN_2P
    rated: fr.derive.Operating | None


@fr.unit("demo-supply-box", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def supply_box(d: fr.Design) -> Supply:
    x1 = d.device("X1", P.DEMO_CONN_2P, interface=True)
    operating = d.operating("DEMO-STRING-864V", "string")
    x1.x1.limits(operating=operating)
    return Supply(x1, operating)

from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Io(NamedTuple):
    X7: fr.Device


@fr.unit("demo-board", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def board(d):
    return Io(d.device("X7", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True))


@fr.unit("demo-assembly", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def assembly(d):
    return Io(d.add(board, "U2").X7)  # the board's connector is the assembly's interface too


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
unit = d.add(assembly, "U1")
d.mate(d.device("P1", "DEMO-CONN-2P"), unit.X7)
assert not [f for f in fr.build(d).findings if f.code == "UNIT_BOUNDARY_BYPASSED"]

items.title: Leaving one instance open
items.text:
unused=True on d.device sits inside the unit, so it marks every instance. A switch's spare ports are declared once there: d.device("X2", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True, unused=True). To leave the boundary of one placed instance open, the container names it on d.add. unused=("X1",) takes every boundary function of the device in the unit's field X1. unused=("X1.x1",) takes that one function. A field that holds a tuple of devices takes an index, "X[0]" or "X[0].x1". The bare "X" takes every element. A misspelt field raises and lists the fields. A name that is no boundary raises and lists the boundary functions. A boundary both mated and declared unused still gives UNUSED_CONTRADICTED. The check runs at the unit the unused= is on: a function that unit hands up from a nested unit, and wires across the nested one, is not contradicted.

A field typed fr.Terminal names that terminal's one function: unused=("X1",). A field typed fr.Run or fr.TerminalStrip, bare as "X3", takes every boundary terminal it holds. "X3[3]" takes terminal 3 and "X3[3:5]" takes terminals 3 and 4, counted from 1; a number past the strip's count raises. For example, unused=("X3[3:5]",) marks terminals 3 and 4 of strip X3. A slice on a tuple field raises. "X1[1].f" on a terminal raises, as does ".f" on a strip terminal. A run or strip with no boundary terminal raises, as a device that is no boundary does.

from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Io(NamedTuple):
    X1: fr.Device


@fr.unit("demo-io-board", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first", by="AB")
def board(d):
    return Io(d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True))


class Cabinet(NamedTuple):
    pass


@fr.unit(
    "demo-cabinet",
    revision=1,
    interface_version=1,
    date="2026-01-01",
    text="first release",
    by="AB",
    title="Demo cabinet",
    number="DC-1",
)
def cabinet(c):
    io1 = c.add(board, "U1")
    io2 = c.add(board, "U2", unused=("X1",))
    c.mate(c.device("B1", "DEMO-CONN-2P"), io1.X1)
    return Cabinet()


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
d.add(cabinet, "U1")

The build holds no BOUNDARY_UNCONNECTED and no UNUSED_CONTRADICTED. U1's X1 is mated, and U2's prints N/A in its table only.

items.title: Variants and revised copies
items.text:
A variant is a parameter of your own builders, never a Fransys feature. Fransys has no variant hook, and nothing patches fr.Design. A revised copy of a unit is a factory around @fr.unit: a function that takes the name, the revision and the variant, and returns the decorated unit.

from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Io(NamedTuple):
    X1: fr.Device


def board_unit(name: str, revision: int, *, pins: str = "DEMO-CONN-2P") -> fr.UnitDef[Io]:
    @fr.unit(name, revision=revision, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="issue", by="AB")
    def board(d: fr.Design) -> Io:
        return Io(d.device("X1", pins, interface=True))

    return board


first = board_unit("demo-io-board", 1)
revised = board_unit("demo-io-board-r2", 2, pins="DEMO-CONN-4P")
d = fr.design("demo_parts")
d.add(first, "U1")
d.add(revised, "U2")
assert len(fr.derive.units(fr.build(d).model)) == 2

items.title: Reaching a unit from outside
items.text:
A container reaches a unit's connector through a plug and d.mate(plug, io.X1). Do not wire onto the connector's own pins. A direct wire onto a male or female connector of a nested unit gives the warning CONNECTOR_WIRED_WITHOUT_MATE. A screw terminal has no gender and takes the wire silently. The core lands on the plug's pin (P1[1]), because the plug is what the container's own wiring reaches, and the mate makes plug and connector conduct as one.

A unit built alone, with nothing outside it, leaves its interface unconnected, and BOUNDARY_UNCONNECTED stays silent: an open interface is what the next integrator connects. The finding fires once the unit sits inside something larger and an interface device is neither mated nor unused.

A nested unit with a harness line at one of its interfaces draws on its parent's page as one outline, with its columns above and below it. A unit with none keeps its usual frame. Inside stand only its interfaces, title and revision. Each line-end interface is a connector box on the outline, and the harness plug touches it from outside. The columns feeding top-edge interfaces stand above, and those leaving bottom-edge interfaces stand below. Layout picks each interface's edge. A single-wire interface keeps its column's flow. Harness interfaces split evenly, with supply-heavy ones on top. d.layout.side(u1.bus_in, fr.ABOVE), or fr.BELOW, fixes one interface's edge when the default reads wrong. The group stands at the left of its page and stays whole on one page.

items.title: Tags and places
items.text: Instance tags count up inside their parent, the cabinet unit: -U1, -U2, with no prefix. One level up, in the top design, they print behind the cabinet's own tag: -U1-U2-X1. A circuit, such as one pump's or one string's, is a function block (with d.function(...)), never a place. A place is where units and field devices stand: a room, a site, a ship's hold.

items.title: Task: a board unit in a cabinet
items.text:
The cabinet is the unit that holds the boards. It holds two identical io boards, U1 and U2. A board has one connector the cabinet plugs into and one spare connector left open. Both boards share one release; each instance prints its own tag, so no designation repeats. The same tag twice in one unit gives PRODUCT_DESIGNATION_DUPLICATE. The cabinet is added to the top design.

# easy: board units in a cabinet
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Io(NamedTuple):
    X1: fr.Device


@fr.unit("demo-io-board", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first release", by="AB")
def board(d):
    x1 = d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True)
    d.device("X2", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True, unused=True)
    return Io(x1)


class Cabinet(NamedTuple):
    pass


@fr.unit(
    "demo-cabinet",
    revision=1,
    interface_version=1,
    date="2026-01-01",
    text="first release",
    by="AB",
    title="Demo cabinet",
    number="DC-1",
)
def cabinet(c):
    io1 = c.add(board, "U1")
    io2 = c.add(board, "U2")
    p1 = c.device("P1", "DEMO-CONN-2P")
    p2 = c.device("P2", "DEMO-CONN-2P")
    c.mate(p1, io1.X1)
    c.mate(p2, io2.X1)
    return Cabinet()


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
d.add(cabinet, "U1")

The efficient level builds the same model. The cabinet's boards and plugs come from one loop.

# efficient: board units in a cabinet
from typing import NamedTuple

import fransys as fr


class Io(NamedTuple):
    X1: fr.Device


@fr.unit("demo-io-board", revision=1, interface_version=1, date="2026-01-01", text="first release", by="AB")
def board(d):
    x1 = d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True)
    d.device("X2", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True, unused=True)
    return Io(x1)


class Cabinet(NamedTuple):
    pass


@fr.unit(
    "demo-cabinet",
    revision=1,
    interface_version=1,
    date="2026-01-01",
    text="first release",
    by="AB",
    title="Demo cabinet",
    number="DC-1",
)
def cabinet(c):
    for n in (1, 2):
        io = c.add(board, f"U{n}")
        c.mate(c.device(f"P{n}", "DEMO-CONN-2P"), io.X1)
    return Cabinet()


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
d.add(cabinet, "U1")

A loop of boards can leave the numbers to the build. Give the release a class_code and each instance a name=, the identity its number holds to in later releases.

@fr.unit(
    "demo-io-board",
    revision=1,
    interface_version=1,
    date="2026-01-01",
    text="first release",
    by="AB",
    class_code="U",
)
def numbered_board(d):
    return Io(d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True))


@fr.unit(
    "demo-numbered-cabinet",
    revision=1,
    interface_version=1,
    date="2026-01-01",
    text="first release",
    by="AB",
    title="Numbered cabinet",
    number="NC-1",
)
def numbered_cabinet(c):
    for n in (1, 2):
        c.add(numbered_board, None, name=f"module{n}")
    return Cabinet()


floating = fr.design("demo_parts")
floating.add(numbered_cabinet, "U1")

Check that the cabinet build has no errors.

result = fr.build(d)
assert not [f for f in fr.check(result) if f.severity is fr.Severity.ERROR]

items.title: Recording revisions
items.text:
A unit's revision= only states which revision is current. Earlier entries go in history=, a list of mappings with revision, date, text and created. The decorator writes the history first, then the unit's own entry from date=, text= and by=. If the current revision has no entry, the build reports REVISION_CURRENT_MISSING. Each history entry also takes version. An entry with no version takes the unit's current version, so after a version bump, earlier entries must name their old version.

from typing import NamedTuple

class Io(NamedTuple):
    X1: fr.Device


@fr.unit(
    "demo-io-board",
    revision=2,
    interface_version=1,
    date="2026-02-02",
    text="added a spare connector",
    by="AB",
    history=[{"revision": 1, "date": "2026-01-01", "text": "first release", "created": "AB"}],
)
def board_r2(d):
    return Io(d.device("X1", "DEMO-CONN-2P", interface=True))


d = fr.design("demo_parts")
d.add(board_r2, "U1")

d.revision(revision, date=, text=, created=) writes one history entry of the project itself, the same way, on a design that is not a unit.

fr.release refuses a history entry that names a revision never released, as RELEASE_HISTORY_UNRELEASED. The cutoff is the first entry, in history order (date, then version and revision), that names a released revision. Entries before it are free text, such as an old register's. Each later entry needs a folder under into in its own version, or must be the revision being released. A first release has no folders, so every entry is free. A system release checks the project's history the same way.

items.title: Writing one unit
items.text: fr.write(result, out_dir, unit="demo-io-board") restricts out_dir to that unit's own documents and lists. A unit's release name is the unit= value. The tuple d.add returns, such as io, is not accepted there. To list a model's units, read sorted(fr.derive.units(model)).
